sections.heading: What is Buckets
sections.content: Buckets is an independent native desktop client for Amazon S3 and compatible object storage. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon Web Services. Built with Electron, it runs natively on macOS, Windows, and Linux, providing a rich visual interface for S3 operations without needing the AWS Console or CLI.

sections.heading: Key Features
sections.content: Buckets is packed with features designed to make S3 management fast, secure, and enjoyable.
tips: Multi-platform support (macOS, Windows, Linux)
Secure credential storage with OS-level encryption
Multiple authentication methods (Access Keys, SSO, AWS CLI Browser Login)
Full bucket and object management (create, delete, upload, download, preview)
Code generation for TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python
CloudFront CDN integration for cache invalidation and distribution management
Lambda function builder for serverless workflows
S3 Select SQL queries to query data in-place
Infrastructure as Code export (CloudFormation, Terraform, CDK)
Dark and Light theme support
Real-time cost estimation per bucket

sections.heading: System Requirements
sections.content: Buckets runs on all major desktop operating systems. Below are the minimum requirements to install and run the application.
tips: macOS 10.15 (Catalina) or later
Windows 10 or later
Linux: Ubuntu 18.04+, Fedora 30+, or equivalent distributions
4 GB RAM minimum
Internet connection required for AWS operations

sections.heading: macOS Installation
sections.content: Buckets is distributed as a DMG disk image for macOS. Follow these steps to install it on your Mac.
steps: Download the DMG file from the Buckets website.
Open the downloaded DMG file.
Drag the Buckets icon into the Applications folder.
On first launch, right-click the app and select Open to bypass Gatekeeper.
The app will verify its integrity and launch.

sections.heading: Windows Installation
sections.content: On Windows, Buckets is distributed as an NSIS installer executable.
steps: Download the NSIS installer (.exe) from the Buckets website.
Run the installer.
Choose an installation directory or accept the default location.
Click Install and wait for the installation to complete.
Launch Buckets from the Start Menu or the Desktop shortcut.

sections.heading: Linux Installation
sections.content: Buckets supports multiple Linux package formats. Choose the one that matches your distribution.
steps: AppImage: Download the .AppImage file, run chmod +x Buckets.AppImage, then execute it with ./Buckets.AppImage.
DEB (Debian/Ubuntu): Download the .deb package and install it with sudo dpkg -i s3console.deb.
RPM (Fedora/RHEL): Download the .rpm package and install it with sudo rpm -i s3console.rpm.

sections.heading: Bundled Tools
sections.content: Buckets comes with bundled AWS CLI and Python runtime, so you don't need to install any external dependencies. This ensures consistent behavior across all platforms and avoids conflicts with existing system installations. The bundled tools are isolated within the application directory and do not interfere with any globally installed versions.

sections.heading: Free Trial
sections.content: Buckets offers a 14-day free trial with full access to every feature. No credit card is required to start the trial. You can begin the trial locally on your machine or register with an email address. The trial period is tied to your specific machine, so reinstalling the app will not reset it.
tips: At startup Buckets compares the system clock with the latest time it saw in earlier sessions. A clock more than 10 minutes behind that counts as tampering unless the license server's time confirms the clock is correct, which also clears an earlier flag. An unconfirmed backward jump since the last session pauses a trial on this device until the time is confirmed (turn on automatic date & time and go online); the trial itself is kept. A recorded tamper also blocks starting a new trial and makes licensed copies re-validate with the server; paid licenses are never removed because of the clock.

sections.heading: Activating a License
sections.content: Once you've purchased a license, activating it takes just a few seconds.
steps: Open the license dialog from the top bar or settings.
Enter the email address associated with your purchase.
Enter your license key.
Click Activate.
The app will verify your license with the server and activate it immediately.

sections.heading: License Status
sections.content: Your current license status is always visible via the chip in the top bar. It shows the plan and the days remaining, for example Trial · 5 days, Yearly · 120d, Lifetime, or Monthly · Payment failed. Click it to see the license details; licenses activated with a license key can also deactivate this machine there, freeing the slot for another computer.

sections.heading: Purchasing a License
sections.content: Licenses can be purchased through the Buckets website. Payment is processed securely via Dodo Payments. After a successful purchase, your license key is delivered to your email address. You can then activate the license in the app using the steps above.

sections.heading: How Updates Work
sections.content: Buckets checks for updates automatically every 30 minutes and whenever the application window regains focus. Updates are downloaded in the background from GitHub Releases, so you can continue working without interruption while the latest version is fetched.

sections.heading: Update Notification
sections.content: When a new update is available, a notification banner appears at the top of the application window. The banner shows the new version number and download progress, keeping you informed without interrupting your workflow.

sections.heading: Installing Updates
sections.content: Installing an update is simple and only requires a quick app restart.
steps: Wait for the update to finish downloading (progress is shown in the notification banner).
Click "Restart & Update" when prompted.
The app will close, install the update, and relaunch automatically.
Your session and credentials are preserved across the update.
tips: Updates are signed and verified for security.
You can continue working while updates download in the background.

sections.heading: Profile & License
sections.content: Open the profile menu (your avatar in the top-right corner) and choose Profile & license to see who the app is activated for, your plan, and trial status. The same dialog lets you enter a license key, start a trial, or sign in to your Buckets account.
steps: Click your avatar in the top bar.
Choose Profile & license.
Review the plan, or choose Activate to enter a license key.
tips: Press Cmd+K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) and search for "Profile & license" or "View pricing" to jump straight to these screens.
The installed app version (Buckets v…) is shown at the bottom of the profile menu.

sections.heading: Billing & Invoices
sections.content: Billing & invoices in the profile menu opens the secure customer portal in your browser. There you can download receipts and invoices, update the payment method, and manage or cancel a subscription. Team owners manage seats from the same portal.
tips: Buckets never shows or stores card details — payments are handled by the portal.
If a payment fails, the subscription is in its grace period, or a canceled subscription ends within 14 days, a banner in the app offers Update payment method, which opens the portal.

sections.heading: Logging Out
sections.content: Log out appears in the profile menu once you are signed in to a Buckets account or hold an active paid license. You are asked to confirm first. Logging out ends the Buckets account session and clears cached user data on this device; saved AWS connection settings are kept so you can sign back in quickly.
tips: Log out does not delete anything in AWS.

Log out does not revoke Drop Zone pages you already generated or hosted. Pages signed with temporary credentials stop working when those credentials expire; pages signed with long-lived access keys keep working until the zone expires. Delete or pause the zone to remove its hosted pages.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The Legal view shows the Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy, and End-User License Agreement that ship with this version of Buckets, so you can read them offline. Open it from the profile menu (Legal) or the command palette.

sections.heading: Reading a Document
sections.content: Pick a document in the left navigation (or from the selector on narrow windows). Links inside a document open in your browser. The newest published versions are always available on buckets.serverlesscreed.com via the external link at the top of the view.
tips: Press Cmd+K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) and search for "Privacy Policy", "Terms" or "EULA" to open a specific document directly.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: AWS Access Keys are the most direct way to connect Buckets to your AWS account. This method requires an IAM user with programmatic access enabled and the appropriate S3 permissions attached. It is ideal for individual developers and quick setups where you have direct control over your IAM credentials.

sections.heading: Creating a Profile
sections.content: Setting up an Access Key profile only takes a moment.
steps: Click the "+" button in the top bar or click "Use Access Keys" in the sidebar.
Enter a profile name to identify this account (e.g., "Production" or "Dev Account").
Enter your AWS Access Key ID.
Enter your Secret Access Key.
Select your preferred AWS region from the dropdown.
Optionally enter a Session Token if you are using temporary credentials from AWS STS.
Click Create Profile.

sections.heading: Credential Security
sections.content: Your credentials are encrypted using Electron's safeStorage API and stored locally on your machine. They never leave your device or get transmitted to any third-party servers. The encryption is tied to your operating system's keychain (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, libsecret on Linux), ensuring that only your OS user account can decrypt them.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Connect to AWS using your organization's IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO). This is the recommended method for enterprise environments with centralized identity management, as it leverages your organization's existing identity provider and access policies.

sections.heading: SSO Login Flow
sections.content: The SSO login process uses a secure device authorization flow through your browser.
steps: Click "Use AWS SSO" in the sidebar or select SSO from the auth switcher in the top bar.
Enter your AWS SSO Start URL (e.g., https://my-org.awsapps.com/start).
Select your Identity Center region from the dropdown.
Click Start SSO Login.
A device authorization code is displayed and your default browser opens automatically.
Authorize the device in your browser by confirming the code.
Select the AWS account you want to access from the list.
Choose a permission set (role) for that account.
Name your profile and select a default region.
Click Complete Setup.

sections.heading: Refreshing SSO Tokens
sections.content: SSO tokens have a limited lifespan and will eventually expire. When your token expires, Buckets will prompt you to re-authenticate through the browser. The re-authentication process is quick since your browser may still have an active session with your identity provider.
tips: SSO tokens typically expire after 8 hours depending on your organization's configuration.
You can save multiple SSO profiles for different accounts and roles within the same organization.
The SSO Start URL is provided by your AWS administrator.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Use the AWS CLI's browser-based login to authenticate with any credential type, including MFA-protected accounts and federated roles. Buckets uses an isolated environment for CLI login, so it will never read from or modify your global AWS CLI configuration.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.content: AWS CLI v2.32.0 or later must be installed on your system. Buckets checks the installed version on startup and will notify you if it is too old or missing. You can download the latest AWS CLI from the official AWS documentation.

sections.heading: Login Flow
sections.content: The CLI Browser Login delegates authentication entirely to your browser, supporting all AWS auth mechanisms.
steps: Click "Browser CLI Login" in the sidebar or select CLI from the auth switcher.
Select your desired AWS region.
Click Start Login.
Your default browser opens to the AWS login page.
Complete the authentication in your browser (supports MFA, SSO, SAML federation, and more).
The app automatically detects when login is complete.
Your credentials are securely captured and you're connected.

sections.heading: Isolated Environment
sections.content: Buckets creates a sandboxed AWS configuration directory specifically for CLI login. This means your existing AWS CLI profiles, configuration files, and credentials in ~/.aws/ are never read or modified. The isolated environment is managed entirely within the app's data directory.
tips: CLI login supports all AWS auth methods including SAML and OIDC federation.
The login process has a 5-minute timeout for security.
Your global ~/.aws/config and ~/.aws/credentials are never modified.

Whenever a credential renewal returns new keys, Buckets checks them with STS GetCallerIdentity first. If the account or principal changed (for example, someone signed in as another user), the new keys are refused and the session must sign in again. The background upload worker renews its own credentials separately.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Buckets supports managing multiple AWS accounts and profiles simultaneously. You can configure profiles using any combination of authentication methods and switch between them instantly without re-entering credentials.

sections.heading: Switching Profiles
sections.content: Switching between configured profiles is seamless.
steps: Click the profile dropdown in the top bar.
Select the profile you want to switch to.
The app validates the credentials and loads the buckets for that profile.
The sidebar updates with the new account's buckets.

sections.heading: Adding Multiple Profiles
sections.content: You can add as many profiles as you need, using any authentication method for each one. Every profile stores its credentials independently with full encryption. This makes it easy to manage development, staging, and production environments side by side, or to work across different AWS organizations.

sections.heading: Auto-Login
sections.content: On app restart, Buckets automatically logs in with the last profile you used. Credentials are persisted securely between sessions, so you can get back to work immediately without any manual re-authentication (unless your SSO token or session token has expired).
tips: Each profile can use a different authentication method.
The active profile name is always shown in the top bar.
Deleting a profile removes its credentials from secure storage permanently.

sections.heading: Switching from the Command Palette
sections.content: Every saved account appears in the command palette as "Switch to <label>". Search for the label or the region to switch without opening a menu.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The auth method switcher provides a quick way to change how you connect to AWS without navigating away from your current view. It is accessible from the top bar and lets you jump directly into any authentication flow.

sections.heading: Using the Switcher
sections.content: The switcher is designed for fast, frictionless access.
steps: Look for the auth method indicator in the top bar.
Click it to open the switcher dropdown.
Select Access Keys, SSO, or CLI Login.
Follow the corresponding authentication flow to connect.

sections.heading: When to Use Each Method
sections.content: Access Keys: Best for direct IAM user credentials and the simplest setup. Ideal for personal accounts and quick access. SSO (IAM Identity Center): Best for enterprise environments with centralized identity management and role-based access. CLI Browser Login: Best when you need MFA, federated roles, SAML/OIDC integration, or other complex authentication flows that go beyond static credentials.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Account tabs work like browser tabs for your saved AWS accounts. Each tab remembers the bucket and folder you were browsing, so you can jump between accounts without losing your place. Only one account's credentials are active at a time; switching tabs switches the active credentials.

sections.heading: Using Tabs
sections.content: Click a tab to activate that account. A green dot marks the live account. SSO and CLI-login tabs show a session timer that turns amber when five minutes or less remain and red when the session has expired — click the timer to sign in again.
steps: Click + at the end of the tab bar.
Pick a saved account, or add a new access-key, AWS CLI or AWS SSO profile.
Click any tab later to return to that account and its last location.

sections.heading: Closing Tabs
sections.content: Closing a tab also removes that saved account from Buckets. If you close the active tab, Buckets moves to the neighbouring tab. Tabs only store account ids, bucket names and prefixes on this device — never credentials.
tips: To keep an account but hide its tab, switch away instead of closing it.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Advanced features › Saved accounts (the Accounts tab in Browse › More › Advanced features) shows the current session — auth method, profile, region and the first characters of the access key — and every saved account.

sections.heading: Saving and Switching
sections.content: Choose Save Current, give the account a label, and the current credentials become a saved account. Each saved account has Switch (re-authenticates if the session expired) and Delete. Rows show the region, profile and when the account was last used.
tips: Saved accounts are stored encrypted on this device.
Press Cmd+K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) and search for "Switch to" followed by an account label to change accounts from anywhere.

sections.heading: Opening Auth Doctor
sections.content: Auth Doctor explains in plain language why a sign-in works or fails and suggests one fix per finding. Open it from the command palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K → “Auth doctor”), from the “Run Auth Doctor” action on an invalid-credentials notification, or from the “Why? Run Auth Doctor” link next to a sign-in error. When opened from an error, the error itself is decoded first.

sections.heading: What It Checks
sections.content: Diagnose the active session, or pick any profile from ~/.aws/config and ~/.aws/credentials to test it before signing in. Every check is read-only; the only AWS call is the free STS GetCallerIdentity.
steps: Credential source: long-term keys, temporary keys with a session token, IAM Identity Center (sso_session or legacy), aws login, an assume-role chain (each hop is listed), MFA roles, web identity, or credential_process (only the executable name is shown).
Environment: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_PROFILE, AWS_CONFIG_FILE, AWS_CA_BUNDLE, HTTPS_PROXY and similar variables that change behaviour between Buckets and the AWS CLI.
Expiry: session credentials, the SSO portal token, the SSO client registration, and whether a refresh token exists.
SSO cache: whether the AWS CLI SSO cache for a profile can still mint credentials without a new browser sign-in.

Reachability: STS, S3 and (for SSO) the Identity Center OIDC and portal endpoints, or the S3-compatible endpoint — through the same TLS and proxy settings the app uses. Failures are classified as certificate, DNS, timeout, refused, reset or proxy errors.
Clock skew: the AWS Date header is compared with this computer's clock. AWS rejects signatures more than five minutes off.
Identity: the account and ARN returned by STS. For S3-compatible endpoints, an optional signed ListBuckets verifies the keys after a cost confirmation.

sections.heading: Decoding AccessDenied
sections.content: AWS's newer 403 messages name the policy type that denied a request — identity-based policy, resource-based (bucket) policy, service control policy (SCP), resource control policy (RCP), permissions boundary, session policy or VPC endpoint policy — and whether it was an explicit Deny or a missing Allow. Auth Doctor and the Permission diagnosis panel parse the principal, action, resource and (when AWS includes it) the denying policy ARN, then tell you who can fix it: you, the bucket owner, or your Organizations administrator.

sections.heading: Copying a Redacted Report
sections.content: Copy redacted report produces plain text you can paste into a ticket. Secret access keys, session tokens, bearer/JWT tokens, proxy passwords and presigned signatures are removed, access key IDs are shortened to their first and last four characters, and your home folder is replaced with ~. Account IDs and role ARNs are kept because support needs them.

sections.heading: Custom CA Bundle
sections.content: Self-hosted MinIO, Ceph RGW or Garage servers and TLS-inspecting corporate proxies often use certificates from a private authority. Open ⌘K → “TLS & proxy settings” (or the “Private CA or self-signed certificate” section of the S3-compatible connection form), enter the endpoint URL and choose a PEM file. Buckets validates the file (certificates only — a file containing a private key is rejected), shows each certificate's subject and expiry, and trusts it in addition to the built-in authorities for that endpoint only. Only the file path is stored.

sections.heading: Allow Self-Signed (Insecure)
sections.content: As a last resort for a lab server you control, “Allow self-signed certificate (insecure)” accepts a certificate no authority signed. It requires confirming a warning, is scoped to the endpoint's host (and its bucket subdomains), still checks the hostname and validity dates, and is refused for every AWS-owned domain both when saving and when connecting. Prefer a custom CA bundle.

sections.heading: AWS CA Bundles
sections.content: AWS connections follow the AWS CLI: the AWS_CA_BUNDLE environment variable wins, otherwise ca_bundle in the active profile's section of ~/.aws/config is used. The bundle is added on top of the default trust store for AWS service, STS and IAM Identity Center requests.

sections.heading: Proxy
sections.content: By default Buckets honours HTTPS_PROXY / HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY from its environment. Choose Manual to enter a proxy URL and bypass list, or No proxy to always connect directly. Proxy credentials are never stored: for an authenticated proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY=http://user:password@host:port in the environment that launches Buckets. Changes rebuild the active S3, upload-worker, SSO and saved-account clients immediately. Auth Doctor warns when your operating system routes AWS through a proxy that Buckets is not using.

sections.heading: Bucket List
sections.content: All buckets for your current AWS account are listed in the left sidebar. Click any bucket to select it and view its contents in the main panel. The bucket list is loaded automatically when you connect with a profile and displays every bucket your credentials have permission to list.

sections.heading: Region Display
sections.content: The active AWS region is shown as a badge in the top bar, giving you immediate visibility into which region you are operating in. Buckets are listed regardless of their region, so you can access all of your S3 storage from a single view.

sections.heading: Refreshing
sections.content: Click the refresh icon in the sidebar header to reload the bucket list. This is useful after creating or deleting buckets externally through the AWS Console, CLI, or another tool. The refresh fetches the latest bucket list directly from AWS.

sections.heading: Basic Setup
sections.content: Creating a new S3 bucket in Buckets is straightforward.
steps: Click the "+" icon in the sidebar header.
Enter a globally unique bucket name.
Select the AWS region where the bucket should be created.
Click Create Bucket.

sections.heading: Advanced Options
sections.content: When creating a bucket, you can configure several advanced options to tailor it to your use case. Versioning keeps multiple versions of objects so you can recover from accidental overwrites or deletions. Block Public Access shows a master switch plus the four individual settings (block new public ACLs, ignore public ACLs, block public bucket policies, restrict public buckets); all four are on by default. The master switch turns all four on or off, and it shows on only while all four are on. Encryption defaults to SSE-S3 (AES-256) but can be configured to use SSE-KMS with a custom key for stricter compliance requirements. Object Lock enables immutable object storage for regulatory and compliance needs. Static Website Hosting allows the bucket to serve static content directly via an HTTP endpoint.

sections.heading: Bucket Naming Rules
sections.content: S3 bucket names must follow specific rules. Names must be globally unique across all AWS accounts worldwide. They must be between 3 and 63 characters long. Only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens are allowed. Names must start with a letter or number. Names cannot be formatted as an IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.1).
tips: Enable versioning for production buckets to prevent accidental data loss.
Block Public Access is recommended unless you specifically need public access.
Choose a region close to your users for lower latency and better performance.

sections.heading: How to Delete
sections.content: Deleting a bucket permanently removes it from your AWS account.
steps: Right-click the bucket in the sidebar, or click the three-dot menu on the bucket.
Select "Delete Bucket" from the context menu.
Type the bucket name to confirm the deletion.
Click Delete.

sections.heading: Important Notes
sections.content: The bucket must be empty before it can be deleted. When the Delete dialog opens it lists what the bucket still holds; if it isn't empty, Delete is disabled and Empty first opens the Empty Bucket dialog. Deletion is permanent and cannot be undone. Once deleted, the bucket name becomes available for other AWS accounts to claim, though there may be a short delay before it can be reused.
tips: Consider emptying the bucket first using the Empty Bucket option.
Bucket names cannot be reused immediately after deletion due to AWS propagation delays.

sections.heading: How to Empty
sections.content: Emptying a bucket removes all objects while keeping the bucket itself intact.
steps: Right-click the bucket in the sidebar, or click the three-dot menu on the bucket.
Select "Empty Bucket" from the context menu.
Confirm the operation in the confirmation dialog.
Wait for all objects to be deleted.

sections.heading: Versioned Buckets
sections.content: For buckets with versioning enabled, the empty operation removes all object versions including delete markers. This ensures the bucket is truly empty and ready for deletion if needed. This is a bulk operation that may take considerable time for large buckets with many versions.
tips: This operation cannot be undone. All objects and versions will be permanently removed.
For very large buckets, the process runs in the background so you can continue working.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Buckets estimates each bucket's monthly storage cost from CloudWatch storage metrics. This gives you a quick view of storage spend without leaving the application or opening the AWS Billing console. For what AWS actually billed, use Cost Explorer (Bucket Settings › Costs).

sections.heading: Viewing Costs
sections.content: Cost information is available directly from the sidebar.
steps: Click the dollar icon next to any bucket in the sidebar.
A dropdown appears showing the estimated monthly cost.
View the cost breakdown by storage class (Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier, etc.).
See the total bucket size and region information.

sections.heading: How Costs are Calculated
sections.content: Costs are estimated from CloudWatch's BucketSizeBytes metric for each storage class present in the bucket, multiplied by bundled list prices for the bucket's Region. S3 publishes this metric once a day with a 24–48 hour lag, so the estimate trails the real bucket size: a new bucket shows no data until its first datapoint, and a datapoint older than 72 hours is labelled stale. The estimate excludes request charges, data transfer fees, and retrieval fees, so your actual AWS bill may differ. The estimate is intended to give you a quick directional understanding of storage costs.
tips: Costs are estimates based on the latest published storage metric and may not match your actual AWS bill exactly.
The estimate updates each time you open the cost dropdown for that bucket.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Bucket properties is a read-only summary sheet for one bucket. Open it from the bucket's … menu in the sidebar, or from the command palette while the bucket is selected. Data loads only while the sheet is open.

sections.heading: What It Shows
sections.content: Identity: name, ARN and region with copy buttons, plus an Open in AWS Console link. Storage: size and estimated monthly cost (shown as unpublished when AWS has no metric yet) with a storage-class breakdown. Security: versioning state, Public Access Block (Fully blocked only when all four settings are on), whether a bucket policy is attached, and ACL grants with a warning for public grantees. Lifecycle & Replication: rule counts and notification targets. Access & Hosting: CORS rules and static website status. Tags: the bucket's tags.
tips: Use the sheet as a quick audit before changing settings — every value links to the setting you would edit.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The All Accounts view lists buckets from every saved account in one sidebar, grouped by account. It needs at least two saved accounts; until then the toggle is hidden.

sections.heading: Using the View
sections.content: In Browse, click the layers icon next to the Buckets heading (or run "Toggle All Accounts bucket view" from the command palette). Each account group shows its label, auth type, a check on the active account and its bucket count. Click a bucket in another account and Buckets switches credentials first, then opens it and returns to the single-account list.
tips: Accounts are listed in parallel with a 15-second limit each, so one slow or failing account never blocks the others.
Results are cached for one minute; use Refresh to reload.

sections.heading: Table View
sections.content: Objects are displayed in a table with columns for Name, Size and Last modified. Rows appear in the order S3 returns them (folders, then keys in UTF-8 order). Click a column header to sort the loaded rows by name, size or date; folders always stay above files. Arrow keys, Page Up/Down, Home and End move between rows, Enter opens the focused row and Shift+Arrow extends the selection.

sections.heading: Navigation
sections.content: Double-click a folder to navigate into it and view its contents. Use the breadcrumb trail at the top of the main panel to jump back to any parent folder in the hierarchy. Click the up arrow button to go directly to the parent directory. Navigation is instant and does not require a full page reload.

sections.heading: Pagination
sections.content: By default Browse scrolls continuously: it lists 1,000 keys per ListObjectsV2 request and fetches the next page as you near the bottom, rendering only the rows on screen so 100,000+ loaded rows stay smooth. The footer shows how many objects are loaded and whether more are available. Prefer fixed pages? Switch the footer toggle to Pages for the classic 100-row Previous/Next list; the choice is remembered.

sections.heading: Upload Methods
sections.content: Buckets offers two convenient ways to upload files. You can click the Upload button in the toolbar to open the native file picker, or you can drag and drop files directly onto the object list from your system's file explorer.

sections.heading: Upload Features
sections.content: Uploads start immediately and provide full progress tracking.
steps: Click Upload in the toolbar or drag files onto the main area.
Select the files or folders you want to upload.
The upload begins immediately with real-time progress tracking.
Large files automatically use multipart upload for reliability and speed.
Failed uploads can be retried on the next app restart.

sections.heading: Folder Uploads
sections.content: You can upload entire folder structures and Buckets will preserve the hierarchy. The folder tree is translated into S3 key prefixes, so a file at photos/vacation/beach.jpg in your local folder will be stored with the same path in S3.
tips: Multipart upload kicks in automatically for files over 5 MB for improved reliability.
You can upload multiple files and folders simultaneously.
Drag and drop works directly from your system's file explorer.

sections.heading: Progress Panel
sections.content: A progress sheet at the bottom of the screen shows all active and recent uploads. It slides into view when uploads begin and provides a comprehensive overview of every transfer in progress.

sections.heading: Features
sections.content: The progress panel includes per-file progress bars with percentage completion, upload speed and file size display for each transfer, status indicators showing whether each file is uploading, completed, or encountered an error, the ability to cancel individual uploads or cancel all active uploads at once, and auto-refresh of the bucket contents when uploads complete.

sections.heading: Canceling Uploads
sections.content: Click the X button next to any file in the progress panel to cancel its upload. To stop all active uploads at once, use the "Cancel All" button at the top of the progress panel. Canceled uploads free up bandwidth immediately for any remaining transfers.

sections.heading: How to Download
sections.content: Downloading objects from S3 is simple and supports full progress tracking.
steps: Navigate to the object you want to download.
Click the download icon on the object's row in the table.
Choose a save location in the system file dialog.
The file downloads with progress tracking for large files.

sections.heading: Download Features
sections.content: You can also initiate downloads from the preview modal using the download button. Downloads display progress indicators for large files so you can track their status. The downloaded file is saved to the exact location you choose in the save dialog.

sections.heading: Editing an Object in a Local App
sections.content: Edit in place opens an object in the app your computer uses for that file type and uploads it back to the same key every time you save.
steps: Open the object's More actions menu and choose Edit in local app, or select the object and run "Edit selected object in local app" from the command palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K).

Review the cost and permission summary. It shows the download size, that every save overwrites the object on S3 (on a versioned bucket earlier versions stay recoverable, on an unversioned bucket the previous content is replaced for good), and how many requests each save makes: 1 HEAD and 1 PUT up to 5 MB, or 1 HEAD and a multipart upload (one request per part plus 2) above that. For Standard-IA and One Zone-IA objects it notes that each saved version is billed for at least 30 days, and 90 days for Glacier Instant Retrieval.

Buckets downloads the object to a private folder that only your user account can read (on Windows in your local, non-roaming AppData; the Microsoft Store version uses a "Buckets edits" folder in your Downloads folder instead, because Store apps' AppData files are hidden from other apps such as Word) and opens it with your default app. The download's progress shows in the Transfers panel, and clicking Edit again while it downloads doesn't start a second copy. Only documents, text and code, images, PDFs, audio and video, and Office files without macros (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx, .odt, .ods, .odp, .rtf) are opened this way; other types, including scripts (.js, .py, .sh, .ps1, .bat), macro-enabled or legacy Office files (.docm, .xlsm, .doc, .xls, .ppt) and files without an extension, are refused: download them instead. On Windows, Office and PDF copies are marked as coming from the internet, so Office opens them in Protected View; click Enable Editing once to edit and save.

Edit and save as usual. Each save is uploaded through the normal upload path, so it appears in the Transfers panel with checksum verification. Retry on such a row retries through the edit session (still conditional, keeping the object's attributes); if the object changed on S3 the row offers Resolve conflict instead. Every save, Overwrite and Save mine as copy is recorded in the local audit log (Operate → Guardrails → Audit) with the bucket, key and outcome, never the file's content.

When you are done, open the Transfers panel and click Stop next to the file. The watcher stops and the temporary copy is deleted. If a save hasn't reached S3 yet (including a save you made while the session was paused), you are asked whether to upload your changes first, discard them, or cancel. Discarding while a save is uploading cancels that upload first; if it had already finished, you are told your save reached S3.

sections.heading: What Is Preserved
sections.content: Each upload keeps the object's Content-Type, user metadata, tags, storage class, server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS key and bucket key), Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Expires and website redirect. If the object's tags can't be read when the session starts, you are told that saves will carry no tags. Not copied, and shown in the session when they apply: ACL grants (saves never set an ACL, so an object made public through its ACL becomes private), archive storage classes (a restored Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive object is saved as Standard, so you are not charged a minimum archive duration per save), and Object Lock legal holds and retention (the bucket's default retention, if any, applies to each new version).

sections.heading: Conflicts
sections.content: Before each upload Buckets checks the object's ETag on S3. If it differs from the version you opened (or last saved), someone else changed or deleted the object, and nothing is uploaded. On AWS the upload itself is also conditional, so a change that lands while your save is uploading is caught too; S3-compatible providers get the check before the upload only. A dialog lets you Overwrite their version, Keep theirs (your local file is replaced with the version on S3), or Save mine as copy (your file is uploaded next to the original as "name (edited <timestamp>).ext" and the session continues on the copy). Overwrite replaces only the version the dialog showed — with the same check before the upload on S3-compatible providers — and reopens the dialog if it changed again. If the copy fails to upload, Retry uploads the copy again. After a crash, a save that had already reached S3 is recognised as yours, not reported as a conflict.

sections.heading: Limits and Restarts
sections.content: Edit in place is not available for folders, archived Glacier or Deep Archive objects (restore them first), objects larger than 1 GB, or profiles in read-only mode. Open sessions survive an app restart but come back paused: click Resume next to the file in the Transfers panel to watch it again, and a save that was not uploaded yet — including one made while the session was paused or the app was closed — is uploaded then. If the app closed during a large save, that upload is not finished automatically at the next sign-in; it waits for your Resume. Paused sessions with unsaved changes light the dot on the ⋯ menu, and at startup a notice offers to review them. Signing out or switching profiles pauses the sessions opened with the previous sign-in, and cancels a save that is still uploading (it is kept for Resume, never finished or retried under the new sign-in); they only resume with that same sign-in, including the same AWS account and role. If an upload fails, the session shows Needs attention with a Retry button. On Windows, if another app has the file open when you choose Keep theirs, the version on S3 is saved next to your file as "name (S3 version).ext" so you can close the file and try again. When you quit with no unsaved uploads or unresolved conflicts, all temporary files are deleted; a file whose content isn't on S3 yet, or that another app still has open, is kept so the next launch can finish, and the quit dialog (and Restart & Install) names those files first — also when you quit from the tray or, on Windows and Linux, by closing the window. If a temporary file can't be deleted when you stop a session, its path is shown so you can remove it yourself.

commands.title: Edit selected object in local app

sections.heading: Single Object Deletion
sections.content: To delete a single object, follow these steps.
steps: Click the delete icon on the object's row in the table.
Confirm the deletion in the confirmation dialog.
The object is permanently removed from the bucket.

sections.heading: Batch Deletion
sections.content: To delete multiple objects at once, select them using the checkboxes on each row, then click the delete button in the toolbar. All selected objects will be removed in a single batch operation. This is much faster than deleting objects one by one for large cleanup tasks.

sections.heading: Folder Deletion
sections.content: Deleting a folder recursively removes all objects that share that prefix. This includes all nested files and subfolders within the folder. Since S3 folders are virtual constructs based on key prefixes, deleting a folder is equivalent to deleting every object whose key starts with that folder path.
tips: Deletion is permanent unless versioning is enabled on the bucket.
With versioning enabled, deleted objects can be restored by removing the delete marker.

sections.heading: How to Create
sections.content: Creating a folder provides a way to organize your objects within a bucket.
steps: Click the Create Folder button in the toolbar.
Enter the folder name.
Click Create.
The folder appears in the current directory immediately.

sections.heading: How Folders Work in S3
sections.content: Amazon S3 does not have a true folder or directory system. Instead, a "folder" is represented as a zero-byte object with a trailing slash in its key name (e.g., "photos/"). Buckets displays these as navigable folders for convenience, providing a familiar file-explorer experience on top of S3's flat key-value storage model.

sections.heading: Supported Formats
sections.content: Buckets supports in-app previews for a wide range of file formats. Images: PNG, JPG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, BMP, SVG. Video: MP4, WebM. Audio: MP3, WAV, OGG. Text: TXT, JSON, XML, HTML, CSS, JS, TS, Markdown, YAML. Files in unsupported formats will display their metadata without a content preview.

sections.heading: Using Preview
sections.content: The preview modal provides a rich view of your file's content and metadata.
steps: Click the preview (eye) icon on any object's row in the table.
The preview modal opens showing the file content rendered appropriately for its type.
View file metadata including size, MIME type, last modified date, and ETag.
Use the action buttons to download, share via presigned URL, or copy the S3 ARN.

sections.heading: Preview Actions
sections.content: From the preview modal, you can perform several actions. Download the file directly to your machine. Generate a presigned URL for sharing the file with others. Copy the object's S3 ARN to your clipboard for use in IAM policies, CLI commands, or Infrastructure as Code templates.
tips: Text files are truncated to 2,000 characters in the preview for performance.
Unsupported file types display metadata only without a content preview.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Presigned URLs provide temporary, shareable access to private S3 objects. They grant time-limited download access without requiring the recipient to have AWS credentials, making them ideal for sharing files with teammates, clients, or external partners.

sections.heading: Generating a URL
sections.content: Creating a presigned URL takes just a few clicks.
steps: Click the share icon on an object's row in the table, or use the share button in the preview modal.
Select the expiration duration, ranging from 1 minute to 7 days.
Click Generate.
The presigned URL is generated and ready to copy.

sections.heading: Sharing
sections.content: Click Copy to copy the presigned URL to your clipboard. Anyone with the URL can download the object until it expires, without needing any AWS credentials. The URL encodes your signing credentials, the target object, and the expiration timestamp into a single shareable link.
tips: Use short expiration times for sensitive data to minimize the exposure window.
Presigned URLs include your credentials in the signature, so avoid sharing them with untrusted parties.
The maximum presigned URL duration is 7 days, which is an AWS-imposed limit.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Upload from URL pulls a file from an http or https address straight into the current folder of the selected bucket. Open it from Upload › Directly from URL, Browse › More › Upload from URL, or the command palette.

sections.heading: Using Upload from URL
sections.content: Enter the source URL. Save as is filled in from the URL's file name until you edit it; it cannot contain a slash. Optional custom headers (one Name: value per line, # for comments) are sent to the source server.
steps: Paste the source URL.
Check the file name.
Add headers under Advanced if the source needs them.
Review the cost summary and start the upload.
tips: Up to five redirects are followed; an Authorization header is dropped when a redirect leaves the original site.
The file is spooled privately on this computer first, so interrupted uploads can resume. The spool is removed afterwards.

Source errors such as HTTP 404/410 or 401/403 require you to correct the URL or headers and explicitly retry. These failed transfers are not labelled Resumable and are not automatically retried after restart. Transient network, rate-limit, and server errors remain retryable.
Large files use multipart upload automatically. Progress appears in the normal upload list.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: S3 has no rename operation, so Buckets copies the object to the new key and deletes the original only after the copy is verified. Open Rename from an object's More actions menu, or from the command palette with the object open in the Inspector.

sections.heading: Rules
sections.content: Rename keeps the object in its current folder — the new name cannot contain a slash. Names cannot be empty or contain control characters, and the full key must stay within 1,024 bytes. Changing the file extension shows a warning with an option to keep the original extension. Objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Deep Archive or the archive tiers must be restored before they can be renamed.
tips: Objects of 5 GB and more are copied with multipart copy and show part-by-part progress.
If the target name already exists, the error appears under the name field and nothing is changed.

sections.heading: Rename or Move a Folder
sections.content: A folder is every object under a prefix, so renaming or moving it costs one copy and one delete per object. Use the folder icon on a folder row, or the command palette's “Rename or move this folder” while the folder is open. Enter the new path — change the last part to rename, or the whole path to move — and choose Review move. Buckets pages through the folder with live progress (stopping at 100,000 objects, in which case totals are shown as lower bounds) and shows the object count, bytes, COPY/LIST and HEAD request counts with an estimated request cost for the region, and DELETE requests (free). It warns about objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive (they cannot be copied until restored and stay behind), objects of 5 GB or more (multipart copy), versioned buckets (originals remain as billed noncurrent versions), Object Lock, and keys that already exist at the destination.
steps: Open the folder row's Rename or move folder action.
Edit the new folder path and choose Review move.
Read the counts, cost and warnings, tick the review box and choose Start move.
Confirm the cost and permission review. Follow progress in the Transfers panel.
tips: Each object is copied, verified (full-object checksum, MD5 ETag, or size when neither is available) and only then deleted from the old folder.
Existing destination objects are never overwritten: an identical copy is accepted, anything different is left alone and the source is kept.
Every step is journaled. Pause, a crash or a restart is safe — Resume continues without copying or deleting any object twice.
Objects that could not be moved stay in the old folder and are listed as failures; Retry failed objects runs only those, for example after restoring archived objects.
Read-only profiles can review a move but cannot start or resume one.

sections.heading: One Queue for Every Transfer
sections.content: The Transfers panel lists uploads, downloads, ZIP and folder downloads, folder renames and moves, cross-bucket and cross-profile copies and moves, and Glacier restore requests in one place. Open it from the arrows button in the top bar (it shows how many transfers are running) or from the command palette with “Transfers panel”. Rows are grouped as Active, Needs attention, Paused and Finished, and the panel reads only local application state — opening it never sends an AWS request.
tips: Clear finished removes completed history from every source while keeping anything that can still be resumed.
A retried upload or download replaces its earlier row instead of adding a duplicate.

sections.heading: Speed, ETA and Controls
sections.content: Each row shows bytes and objects transferred, a smoothed speed and an estimated time remaining while it runs. Controls depend on the transfer: cancel or retry single uploads and downloads (a retried download resumes from its partial file); pause, resume or discard ZIP and folder downloads and folder moves; pause, resume, cancel or retry failed objects for cross-bucket jobs. Discarding a job and cancelling a cross-bucket job ask for a second click. Retrying an upload or download shows the cost and permission review first.

sections.heading: Resumable ZIP and Folder Downloads
sections.content: Download ZIP and Download into a folder create a durable job from the exact manifest you reviewed. Every object is streamed to disk (never held in memory), requested with If-Match on the reviewed ETag, and verified by size and — for single-part objects without SSE-KMS — by MD5. A dropped connection continues from the byte offset already on disk. Each verified object is appended to a completion log next to the destination, so after a pause, a crash or an application restart Resume downloads only what is missing. The ZIP is assembled into a .partial file only after every object is verified and is renamed into place only when it contains every entry; a failed object leaves no ZIP behind.
tips: ZIP output needs free space for the staged objects plus the archive; folder output needs space for the objects only. Buckets checks before it starts.
Resume must run under the same AWS profile that started the download.
Discard removes staged data; files already written by a folder download are kept.

sections.heading: Folder Sync Summary
sections.content: Folder Sync keeps its own progress bar and window. The Transfers panel shows a one-line, read-only summary — files synced, speed, time remaining and anything that needs attention — with a shortcut to open Folder Sync.

sections.heading: Reliability Test Suite
sections.content: Transfer behaviour is pinned by automated tests that run against a simulated S3: a connection dropped mid-download resumes from the exact offset on disk; a 64 MiB stream never holds more than a few chunks in memory; a checksum or size mismatch is retried once and then reported, never saved; resuming a ZIP download skips verified objects and never writes a partial archive; and resuming an interrupted folder move neither copies nor deletes any object twice.

sections.heading: Selecting Objects
sections.content: Tick the checkbox on rows and a selection bar appears above the list. Shift+click a second checkbox to select the whole range in between. The header checkbox selects all loaded objects that match the filter — never objects that are not listed yet; the selection bar shows "n items selected of N loaded". Use Load all in the footer first when an action must cover a whole large folder. The command palette can also select all loaded objects or clear the selection. With the Inspector open, a multi-select summary shows the count, total size and storage classes.

sections.heading: Download as ZIP
sections.content: Download ZIP packs the selected files and folders into one archive, or saves them as files in a new folder. Buckets first expands folders and shows a review: object count, total size and the first paths. Choose ZIP or folder, tick the review checkbox and choose where to save. The download then runs in the background and appears in the Transfers panel, where it can be paused and resumed — also after a dropped connection or an application restart. The ZIP is written as a .partial file only after every object has been downloaded and verified, and renamed only when complete.
tips: Up to 1,000,000 objects per download; the review expires after 15 minutes.
Each object is fetched only if it has not changed since the review, and verified by size and, where S3 provides one, by MD5.
Resume downloads only objects that are not yet verified; partially downloaded objects continue from their byte offset.

sections.heading: Bulk Tagging
sections.content: Tag (n) opens the bulk tag editor with three modes: Merge (default) adds or overwrites the tags you enter and can remove listed keys; Set replaces each object's whole tag set; Clear removes all tags. The exact change set is shown before anything is written.
tips: AWS allows 10 tags per object, keys up to 128 characters and values up to 256.
Merge reads existing tags first; an object that would exceed 10 tags fails and keeps its tags.
Autocomplete: when the editor opens, Buckets samples the tags of up to 1,000 objects in the bucket and suggests the keys it found and, for each key, its 25 most frequent values.

sections.heading: Metadata & Lock
sections.content: Metadata & lock edits up to 1,000 objects at once. The Metadata tab merges or replaces custom metadata and can override Content-Type and Cache-Control; changes are applied with a conditional self-copy, so an object that changed after the preview is skipped. The Legal hold and Retention tabs apply Object Lock settings (Object Lock must be enabled on the bucket).
tips: Compliance retention cannot be shortened or removed by anyone, including the root user.
Objects larger than 5 GB cannot be rewritten for metadata changes.

sections.heading: Other Bulk Actions
sections.content: Transfer (n) copies or moves the selection to another bucket or profile, Restore (n) restores archived files, and Delete (n) deletes the selection after confirmation.

commands.title: Edit metadata & Object Lock for selection

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The Inspector keeps an object's details and the bucket's permissions on screen next to the file list. Toggle it with Cmd+\ (Ctrl+\) or the Inspector button in the Browse toolbar. With the Inspector open, clicking a file selects it instead of opening the preview.

sections.heading: Object Panel
sections.content: Shows copyable S3 URI, HTTPS URL and ARN, plus size, storage class, dates, ETag, content headers, encryption, checksum, Object Lock, replication, version id and user metadata. Quick actions: Preview, Download, Presign 15m (a 15-minute link copied to the clipboard), Tags, Metadata and Versions. The object's tags can also be edited inline in the panel; S3's limits are checked before saving (at most 10 tags, keys up to 128 and values up to 256 characters, no aws: prefix, no duplicate keys, allowed characters only). Inline editing is disabled for read-only profiles.

sections.heading: Permissions Panel
sections.content: The lower half edits the bucket's ACL, Bucket Policy, Public Access Block and CORS in tabs. Cycle tabs with Cmd+Shift+\ (Ctrl+Shift+\). Full editor opens the complete Access Control dialog, which also includes the IAM policy generator. Drag the divider (or use the arrow keys on it) to resize; the split is remembered.
tips: Unsaved edits are protected — Buckets asks before discarding a policy draft or unsaved ACL, Public Access Block or CORS changes, including when you select a different object.

sections.heading: Policy Editor Workspace
sections.content: On windows at least 760 pixels wide, the Policy tab can switch to a side-by-side layout: a full-height JSON editor with templates, Format, Copy, Delete and Save on one side, and context on the other — object and bucket ARNs, live validation of every statement, saved snapshots, and a Prefixes section listing the bucket's first 50 top-level prefixes with copyable prefix ARNs.

sections.heading: Policy Snapshots
sections.content: Every bucket policy save that S3 confirms is snapshotted locally, from any editor (the Inspector, the Access Control dialog or CloudFront setup), together with the policy it replaced (identical consecutive saves are skipped). Up to 10 snapshots are kept across all buckets. Restoring a snapshot loads it into the editor; choose Save to apply it. Snapshots are a local convenience, not S3 versioning.

sections.heading: Annotations
sections.content: The collapsible Annotations section lists the object's S3 Annotations (AWS-only) the first time you expand it. View shows the content (JSON is pretty-printed); Add annotation and Edit open an editor with a live 1 MiB size guard; Delete asks for confirmation; Query annotations in Athena opens the Athena workbench on the bucket's annotation table. See S3 Annotations for details.

sections.heading: CloudFront URLs
sections.content: When the bucket is an origin of one or more CloudFront distributions, the Inspector lists the object's CloudFront URLs: alternate domain names first, then the *.cloudfront.net domain. Origin paths and cache-behavior routing are respected, so a key outside a distribution's origin path, or routed by a behavior to another origin, gets no URL. Disabled distributions are labelled. The same URL is available from the row's More actions › Copy CloudFront URL.
tips: The list comes from one ListDistributions sweep per bucket, cached for five minutes; it needs cloudfront:ListDistributions.
Hidden for S3-compatible connections.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Amazon S3 Annotations (June 2026) attach named, mutable context to an object: JSON, YAML, XML or plain text that can change at any time without rewriting the object. AWS allows up to 1,000 annotations per object, each up to 1 MiB (1 GB per object). Annotations follow the object through copy and replication and are deleted with it. Buckets shows them in the Inspector's Annotations section. They are an AWS feature, so the section is hidden for S3-compatible connections.

sections.heading: Viewing Annotations
sections.content: Select an object with the Inspector open and expand Annotations. Each row shows the name, size, last-modified time and replication status. Choose the eye button to load the content; JSON is pretty-printed, everything else is shown as text.

sections.heading: Adding and Editing
sections.content: Add annotation asks for a name and content. Names are 1–512 bytes and cannot start with aws or s3. Content must be valid UTF-8 text up to 1 MiB; the editor counts bytes as you type and blocks oversized content. Choose JSON to validate and format the payload. Saving opens the cost and permission review (one PutObjectAnnotation request; annotation storage is billed at S3 Standard rates even when the object is archived), then writes the annotation.
steps: Open the Inspector (Cmd+\ / Ctrl+\) and select an object.
Expand Annotations and choose Add annotation, or view an annotation and choose Edit.
Enter the name and content, then choose Review and save.
Review the cost and permission summary and continue.
tips: Writes are conditional on the object's ETag shown in the Inspector, so an annotation is never attached to an object that was replaced after you loaded it.
Saving an existing name replaces its content; S3 keeps one value per name.
Required IAM action for writes: s3:PutObjectAnnotation. Reads use s3:GetObjectAnnotation; listing and deleting use the ListObjectAnnotations and DeleteObjectAnnotation APIs.
Per-profile read-only mode blocks saving and deleting annotations.

sections.heading: Deleting Annotations
sections.content: Choose the trash button on an annotation and confirm. Only the annotation is removed; the object is unchanged. An enabled annotation table drops the row within about an hour.

sections.heading: Querying in Athena
sections.content: Query annotations in Athena opens the Athena workbench with a query against the bucket's S3 Metadata annotation table, filtered to the selected object (columns bucket, object_key, name and text_value). The table must be enabled first in Bucket settings › Local index › Live S3 Metadata. Athena charges for bytes scanned.
tips: Annotation tables refresh within about an hour; enabling the table on a bucket with existing annotations starts a backfill that can take hours to days.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Search within the currently selected bucket using the search bar integrated into the breadcrumb navigation.

sections.heading: How to Search
sections.content: Use the integrated search bar in the breadcrumb navigation to quickly find files and folders within the current bucket.
steps: Navigate to a bucket.
Click the search icon in the breadcrumb bar or start typing in the search field.
Enter your search query.
Results appear in real-time as you type.
Use arrow keys to navigate results and Enter to select.
Click a result to navigate to that file or folder.

sections.heading: Search Results
sections.content: Results show file/folder icons along with file size. Matching is a case-insensitive key substring across the whole bucket, not just the current folder.
tips: Use keyboard arrows for fast navigation through results.
A live search stops after 500 ListObjectsV2 pages (about 500,000 keys) and says so; use a Local Index for complete results on larger buckets.

sections.heading: Search Sources
sections.content: Search picks its source automatically and labels it under the search box. A Local Index (S3 Inventory ingested into SQLite) whose inventory report was created within the last 24 hours answers as you type: "via Local Index (inventory from 3h ago) · 0 LIST requests". The age counts from the report's own creation time (when S3 scanned the bucket), not from when you imported it, so importing an old weekly report does not make it fresh. Otherwise, if the bucket's S3 Metadata inventory table is active, press Enter to run one Athena query against it after a cost review ("via S3 Metadata table (Athena) · 0 LIST requests"). Without either, search lists the bucket live and shows the bounded request count and price, for example "via ListObjectsV2 · up to 500 requests (≤$0.0025)", replaced by the actual count after the search.
tips: Search live instead bypasses the index when you need state newer than the snapshot.
An index whose inventory report is older than 24 hours is never used silently: search goes live and offers Use stale index.
Global Object Search also answers buckets with a fresh Local Index locally and reports how many LIST requests the rest of the scan used.
Local Index matching is case-insensitive for ASCII letters.

commands.title: How bucket search picks its source

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Search across buckets (the search icon in the top bar) finds objects by key in every bucket of the active account when you do not know where an object lives. For an explicit, reviewed scan across every saved account, use Global Object Search; to jump to features, use the command palette (Cmd+K / Ctrl+K).

sections.heading: Using Search Across Buckets
sections.content: Results are grouped by bucket, up to 50 per bucket.
steps: Click the search icon in the top bar (or run "Search across buckets" from the command palette).
Type part of an object key.
Use the arrow keys or mouse to pick a result.
Press Enter to open its folder in Browse.

sections.heading: Search Features
sections.content: Search starts as you type, can be retried after an error, and closes with Esc.
tips: Each search lists objects in every bucket, which can be billed as S3 LIST requests.
To search inside one bucket, use In-Bucket Search; for millions of objects, use the Local Inventory Index.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Search object-key substrings across saved access-key and active-session SSO accounts without changing the active AWS session. Results are grouped by account and bucket. CLI Login accounts must be searched while active.

sections.heading: How to Search
sections.content: Global Object Search is a bounded live S3 scan. Before it starts, the app shows required permissions and an estimated regional request cost.
steps: Open the Search Across Buckets modal from the tools menu.
Enter at least two characters of an object-key substring.
Review and approve the permission and cost preflight.
Results are grouped by saved account and bucket.
Switch to the result's account before opening an object from a different account.

sections.heading: Use Cases
sections.content: Finding files that may exist in multiple buckets. Locating a specific file when you don't remember which bucket it's in. Auditing file presence across your S3 infrastructure.
tips: Each bucket stops after 10,000 scanned object names or 50 matches; truncated and skipped buckets are reported in Coverage.

Buckets with a Local Index built from an inventory report created in the last 24 hours are searched locally with 0 LIST requests; the result header reports how many buckets used the index and how many LIST requests the live part of the scan made.
A failed or expired saved account is isolated so other accounts can still return results.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The command palette reaches every feature in Buckets from one search box — workspaces, tools, dialogs, and the individual tabs inside them, however deeply they are nested. Open it with Cmd+K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux), or the Jump to… button in the top bar.

sections.heading: Searching
sections.content: Type any part of a feature's name, where it lives, or what it does. Every word must match, so "settings lifecycle" finds Lifecycle rules and "cost tags" finds Bucket tags. Results are grouped by area and ranked, with exact and leading matches first.
tips: Start with > to search commands only, # for buckets, accounts and recent objects, or ? for documentation pages.
Searches match AWS terms too: try "PutBucketRequestPayment"-style words such as requester pays, cloudtrail or terraform.

sections.heading: Nested Features and Breadcrumbs
sections.content: Each result shows a breadcrumb of where the feature lives in the interface, for example Browse › More › Settings under Lifecycle rules. Running it opens that exact place — the Settings dialog on its Lifecycle tab, the Operate workbench scrolled to the Undo window panel, or the CloudFront page with the Create Distribution dialog open.

sections.heading: Context and Scope
sections.content: Some commands act on the selected bucket, the object shown in the Inspector, or the checked rows. The right side of each result shows what it will act on, or "select a bucket first" when something is missing. Running a bucket command without a bucket takes you to Browse and asks you to pick one.

sections.heading: Recents
sections.content: When the search box is empty, the palette shows your recent commands, the workspaces, recently inspected objects and your buckets. Recent commands are kept on this device only. Run "Clear recent objects & commands" to reset both lists.

sections.heading: Opening Documentation
sections.content: Press Shift+Enter (or Shift+click) on any command to open its documentation page instead of running it. Every documentation page is also searchable directly from the palette.

sections.heading: Keyboard Reference
sections.content: Use the arrow keys to move, Enter to run, Shift+Enter for documentation and Esc to close.
tips: Cmd/Ctrl+K — open the palette
↑ / ↓ — move between results
Enter — run
Shift+Enter — open documentation
Esc — close

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The filter bar above the object list narrows the current page with a small expression language. Matching happens instantly on this computer — no AWS requests. The same syntax powers Inventory index search, where it covers the whole bucket.

sections.heading: Fields
sections.content: name (the display name), key (the full S3 key), size, modified, type (file or folder) and class (storage class). A bare word without a field matches the name, as a substring or as a glob when it contains * or ?.

sections.heading: Operators and Logic
sections.content: Use : (contains, or glob with * and ?), =, !=, >, <, >= and <=. Combine terms with AND (also implied between terms), OR, NOT and parentheses. NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR. Quote values with spaces using " or '.

sections.heading: Values and Units
sections.content: Sizes accept B, KB, MB, GB and TB (1 KB = 1,024 bytes). Dates accept relative ages — 30d, 12h, 45m — or an ISO date such as 2026-01-31. modified < 30d means older than 30 days; modified > 7d means changed within the last week. Storage classes compare case-insensitively.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.content: Click ? in the filter bar to insert any example.
tips: *.log
size > 100MB
modified < 30d
modified > 7d AND size > 1MB
name:*.json OR name:*.csv
type = folder
class = STANDARD_IA
NOT name:".tmp"

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Access Control Lists (ACLs) define who can access your bucket and what permissions they have. Buckets provides both canned (preset) and custom ACL configurations.

sections.heading: Canned ACLs
sections.content: Private: Owner gets full control (default). Public Read: Anyone can read objects. Public Read-Write: Anyone can read and write. Authenticated Read: Only authenticated AWS users can read.

sections.heading: Custom ACL Grants
sections.content: For more granular control, you can create custom ACL grants that specify individual grantees and their permissions.
steps: Open the Access Control modal for a bucket (right-click bucket then Access Control).
Go to the ACL tab.
Click Add Grant.
Select a grantee type (Canonical User ID, Email, or Group URI).
Choose permissions (READ, WRITE, READ_ACP, WRITE_ACP, FULL_CONTROL).
Click Save.
tips: AWS recommends using bucket policies instead of ACLs for most use cases.
The 'Everyone' group means anonymous public access.
Canned ACLs replace all existing grants.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Bucket policies are JSON documents that define access permissions for your bucket and its objects. Buckets provides a full JSON editor with syntax highlighting and pre-built templates.

sections.heading: Using Templates
sections.content: Buckets includes ready-to-use policy templates: Public Read (allow anyone to read objects), Restricted IP (limit access to specific IP ranges), CloudFront OAI (allow CloudFront distribution access), Cross-Account (grant access to another AWS account), HTTPS Enforcement (require encrypted connections), VPC Endpoint (restrict access to a specific VPC).

sections.heading: Editing Policies
sections.content: Use the built-in editor to write, modify, or apply bucket policies with full syntax highlighting and validation.
steps: Open Access Control modal for a bucket.
Go to the Bucket Policy tab.
Select a template or write your own JSON policy.
Review the policy in the syntax-highlighted editor.
Click Apply Policy to save.
To remove a policy, click Delete Policy.
tips: Always test policies in a non-production environment first.
Invalid JSON will be rejected with an error message.
Use the policy validator in the AWS Console for complex policies.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Generate IAM policies that can be attached to IAM users, roles, or groups in the AWS Console. These policies control what S3 actions the principal can perform.

sections.heading: Available Templates
sections.content: Read-Only: List and get objects. Read-Write: List, get, and put objects. Full Admin: Full S3 access to the bucket. List Only: list all buckets (s3:ListAllMyBuckets), read the bucket's Region (s3:GetBucketLocation) and list keys in the selected bucket (s3:ListBucket), optionally only under a prefix through an s3:prefix condition; it grants no object read or write. Upload Only: Only put objects, cannot read or delete. Delete Deny: Explicitly deny delete operations.

sections.heading: How to Use
sections.content: Generate and copy IAM policies directly from Buckets for use in the AWS IAM Console.
steps: Open the Access Control modal for a bucket.
Go to the IAM Policy tab.
Select a template that matches your needs.
The generated policy JSON is displayed.
Click Copy to copy it to your clipboard.
Paste the policy into the IAM Console when creating or editing a policy.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Public Access Block provides account-level and bucket-level settings to prevent public access to your S3 resources. These settings override any ACLs or bucket policies that grant public access.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.content: Block New Public ACLs: Prevents setting new ACLs that grant public access. Ignore Existing Public ACLs: Ignores any existing ACLs that grant public access. Block New Public Policies: Prevents setting bucket policies that grant public access. Restrict Public Buckets: Restricts access to buckets with public policies to AWS principals within the same account.

sections.heading: How to Configure
sections.content: Manage public access block settings to control whether your bucket can be made publicly accessible.
steps: Open the Access Control modal for a bucket.
Go to the Public Access Block tab.
Toggle each setting on or off as needed.
Click Save Changes.
tips: These settings are enabled by default on new buckets.
Disabling public access block is required before making a bucket public.
Consider keeping all four settings enabled unless you specifically need public access.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) configuration allows web applications hosted on different domains to access objects in your S3 bucket. This is essential for web apps that load resources directly from S3.

sections.heading: Configuring CORS
sections.content: Set up CORS rules to control which domains, HTTP methods, and headers are allowed when accessing your bucket from a browser.
steps: Open the Access Control modal for a bucket.
Go to the CORS tab.
Add a CORS rule with the allowed origins, methods, and headers.
Configure expose headers and max age if needed.
Click Save CORS Configuration.

sections.heading: Common Configuration
sections.content: A typical CORS rule includes: AllowedOrigins (domains that can access the bucket, e.g. https://myapp.com), AllowedMethods (HTTP methods like GET, PUT, POST, DELETE), AllowedHeaders (request headers the browser can send), ExposeHeaders (response headers the browser can access), MaxAgeSeconds (how long the browser caches the CORS response).
tips: Use '*' for AllowedOrigins only in development, never in production.
CORS rules are evaluated in order and the first match is used.
To remove CORS, click Delete CORS Configuration.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The Security Scanner checks a bucket for public exposure and samples object contents for secrets and personal data. Open it from Browse › More › Security scan or the command palette. Every scan shows a cost and permission review first because it lists and reads objects.

sections.heading: Scan Options
sections.content: Prefix defaults to the current folder (leave it empty for the whole bucket). Max objects is 1–50,000 (default 5,000). Bytes sampled per object is up to 4 MB (default 1 MB), read with ranged requests. You can also check per-object ACLs and include low-severity findings. Object Ownership is read once per scan: on a bucket whose ACLs are disabled (Bucket owner enforced), per-object ACL reads are skipped because object ACLs cannot grant access there. Each run records whether object ACLs were checked, skipped because ACLs are disabled, or incomplete (with how many object ACLs could not be read), and the results say so.
steps: Open the scanner on the bucket.
Adjust the prefix and limits.
Start the scan and approve the cost review.
Filter findings by severity and status.

sections.heading: What It Finds
sections.content: Posture: Block Public Access disabled, public bucket policies and public ACL grants. Secrets: AWS keys, GitHub and Slack tokens, JWTs, private keys and inline passwords. Personal data: US Social Security numbers, card numbers, email addresses, phone numbers and public IPv4 addresses. Evidence is masked before it is stored.

sections.heading: Fixing Findings
sections.content: Posture findings have a Fix button: turn on all four Block Public Access settings, delete a public bucket policy (after confirmation), or set the bucket or object ACL to private. Content findings need a manual fix — open the object, remove the data, then Dismiss the finding. Clear history deletes scan results for the bucket; bucket data is never touched.
tips: Only the first bytes of each object are sampled, so this is a fast check, not a replacement for Amazon Macie.
Results are kept locally so reopening the scanner shows the last scan instantly.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: AWS audit evidence (Browse › More › AWS audit evidence) collects authoritative AWS records about one bucket in three tabs. Refresh reloads everything.

sections.heading: CloudTrail Events
sections.content: Management events from the last 30 days that name the bucket — up to 50 — with the event name, time, identity, source IP, read/write type and error code. Data events (object reads and writes) need a CloudTrail trail or event data store and are not shown here.

sections.heading: Access Analyzer Findings
sections.content: Active findings for the bucket from every active IAM Access Analyzer in the region (up to 50 per analyzer). A warning appears if the region has no active analyzer.

sections.heading: Organization Lens
sections.content: Your account id, the AWS Organization and management account when available, and each S3 Storage Lens configuration with its scope.
