tips: Press Cmd+K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) and search for "CloudTrail events", "Access Analyzer findings" or "Organization Lens" to open a tab directly.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: When a folder cannot be listed because access is denied, the error panel offers Explain this denial. Buckets runs read-only checks and lists the likely causes. No settings are changed.

sections.heading: What Is Checked
sections.content: Buckets infers the S3 action that failed, then probes Public Access Block, Object Ownership, default encryption, Requester Pays and the bucket policy status. It also identifies the caller with STS and, where allowed, simulates the IAM policy for the action.

sections.heading: Reading the Results
sections.content: Each likely cause names the policy layer (identity, resource policy, SCP, permissions boundary, session policy, VPC endpoint, KMS or Requester Pays), the evidence, and a next step. Findings that AWS confirmed directly are marked.
tips: Buckets cannot read SCPs, boundaries, endpoint policies or KMS key policies; CloudTrail and IAM Access Analyzer are the authoritative sources.
Use Run again after changing a policy.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Versioning keeps multiple variants of an object in the same bucket. When enabled, every overwrite or delete creates a new version rather than replacing the original.

sections.heading: Enabling Versioning
sections.content: Enable versioning on a bucket to preserve every version of every object stored in it.
steps: Open Bucket Settings for a bucket.
Go to the Versioning tab.
Use Enable to enable versioning. The switch saves the change immediately.
Wait for the status read from AWS to show Enabled.

sections.heading: Refreshing Versioning Status
sections.content: Use Refresh versioning status after changing versioning in AWS Console, or reopen Bucket Settings. A failed read shows Unknown and disables the switch until the status can be loaded. Disabled is shown only after a successful read confirms versioning has never been enabled. Settings use the selected Region and retry once in the bucket Region when AWS reports a different endpoint.

sections.heading: Working with Versions
sections.content: List all versions of an object to see its history. Restore a previous version to make it the current version. Delete a specific version permanently. Pick two versions and choose Compare to see what changed between them.

sections.heading: Comparing Versions
sections.content: In the versions dialog, tick exactly two versions (delete markers cannot be compared) and choose Compare. For text-like objects — by extension or content type, up to 2 MB each — Buckets shows the request count first (2 GET requests and their estimated price), then fetches both versions and renders a line diff, side by side or unified, with added and removed line counts and a Copy unified diff button. Binary or larger objects get a metadata comparison instead (size, ETag, last modified and storage class from the listing) with no extra requests. The command palette's Compare two versions of this object opens the dialog with the two newest versions preselected.
tips: CRLF and LF line endings compare as equal lines; a file that only changed its line endings shows no differences.
The unified diff on the clipboard uses the two version IDs as its file labels, ready to paste into a ticket or a code review.

sections.heading: Version Suspension
sections.content: You can suspend versioning, which stops creating new versions but preserves existing ones. Previously versioned objects remain accessible.
tips: Versioning cannot be disabled once enabled, only suspended.
Each version is stored as a separate object and incurs storage costs.
Enable versioning before setting up replication.

commands.title: Compare two versions of this object

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Lifecycle rules automatically transition objects between storage classes or expire (delete) them after a specified period. Ideal for cost optimization and data retention policies.

sections.heading: Creating a Rule
sections.content: Define lifecycle rules to automate storage class transitions and object expiration based on age or other criteria.
steps: Open Bucket Settings for a bucket.
Go to the Lifecycle tab.
Click Add Rule.
Enter a rule name and optional prefix filter.
Configure transition actions (e.g. move to Glacier after 30 days).
Configure expiration actions (e.g. delete after 365 days).
Click Save Rule.

sections.heading: Transition Actions
sections.content: Move objects to cheaper storage classes over time: Standard to Standard-IA (after 30+ days), Standard-IA to Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval, or Deep Archive.

sections.heading: Expiration Actions
sections.content: Automatically delete objects after a specified number of days. Can also clean up incomplete multipart uploads and expired delete markers.
tips: Minimum storage duration charges apply when transitioning (e.g. 30 days for Standard-IA).
Use prefix filters to apply rules to specific folders.
Test rules on non-production data first.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Configure S3 to send notifications when specific events occur in your bucket, such as object creation, deletion, or restoration.

sections.heading: Setting Up Notifications
sections.content: Create event notification configurations to trigger actions in response to S3 events.
steps: Open Bucket Settings for a bucket.
Go to the Notifications tab.
Click Add Notification.
Select event types (ObjectCreated, ObjectRemoved, etc.).
Configure optional prefix and suffix filters.
Choose a destination (SNS topic, SQS queue, or Lambda function).
Enter the destination ARN.
Click Save.

sections.heading: Event Types
sections.content: Every event type AWS supports for SNS, SQS and Lambda destinations: ObjectCreated (*, Put, Post, Copy, CompleteMultipartUpload), ObjectRemoved (*, Delete, DeleteMarkerCreated), ObjectRestore (*, Post, Completed, Delete), ReducedRedundancyLostObject, Replication (*, OperationFailedReplication, OperationMissedThreshold, OperationReplicatedAfterThreshold, OperationNotTracked), LifecycleExpiration (*, Delete, DeleteMarkerCreated), LifecycleTransition, IntelligentTiering, ObjectTagging (*, Put, Delete) and ObjectAcl:Put.
tips: The destination resource must have a policy allowing S3 to publish to it.
Notifications are read and saved in the bucket's own Region, even when your profile's default Region is different.
Use prefix/suffix filters to limit which objects trigger notifications.
Each notification configuration must have a unique name.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Replication automatically copies objects from one bucket to another. Cross-Region Replication (CRR) copies to a bucket in a different region. Same-Region Replication (SRR) copies within the same region.

sections.heading: Setting Up Replication
sections.content: Configure replication rules to automatically copy objects to a destination bucket for redundancy, compliance, or latency optimization.
steps: Ensure versioning is enabled on both source and destination buckets.
Open Bucket Settings for the source bucket.
Go to the Replication tab.
Click Add Rule.
Select the destination bucket and region.
Configure an IAM role for replication.
Set optional prefix filters.
Click Save.

sections.heading: Use Cases
sections.content: Compliance requirements for data in multiple regions. Lower latency by replicating data closer to users. Disaster recovery with cross-region copies.
tips: Both source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled.
Existing objects are not replicated, only new objects after rule creation.
Replication does not copy delete markers by default.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: S3 Inventory provides a flat file listing of objects and their metadata on a daily or weekly schedule. Useful for auditing and compliance.

sections.heading: Creating an Inventory
sections.content: Set up an inventory configuration to receive regular reports about the objects in your bucket.
steps: Open Bucket Settings for a bucket.
Go to the Inventory tab.
Click Add Configuration.
Set a name and destination bucket for reports.
Choose frequency (Daily or Weekly).
Select output format (CSV, ORC, or Parquet).
Choose which metadata fields to include.
Click Save.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Monitor your bucket's storage usage and request patterns using CloudWatch metrics and S3 analytics.

sections.heading: Storage Metrics
sections.content: Bucket Settings › Metrics shows the last 14 days of the daily CloudWatch storage metrics: BucketSizeBytes for the storage type you pick (S3 Standard, each Intelligent-Tiering tier, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Glacier classes and more) and NumberOfObjects. A metric with no datapoints shows No data with the reason; S3 reports these metrics daily and they can take up to 48 hours to appear for a new bucket.

sections.heading: Request Metrics
sections.content: Request metrics (all, GET, PUT, DELETE requests and more) are published only for a metrics configuration. Add a configuration with an optional filter (prefix, tag or Access Point ARN), then pick it in Request Metrics together with the metric and, where the metric offers more than one, the statistic. The panel shows the last 14 days at hourly resolution for that configuration's filter.

sections.heading: Analytics
sections.content: The Metrics tab also includes the Storage Class Analyzer (current objects by storage class). Metrics configurations can be listed, created and deleted here, each with an optional prefix, tag or Access Point ARN filter; an Access Point filter must be a full access point ARN.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations to speed up uploads to your bucket over long distances.

sections.heading: Enabling
sections.content: Enable Transfer Acceleration to route uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge location for improved speed.
steps: Open Browse › More › Advanced features for the bucket.
Go to the Acceleration tab.
Turn the Transfer Acceleration switch on; the change is saved when you toggle it.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.content: When enabled, uploads are routed through the nearest CloudFront edge location, then transferred to S3 over Amazon's optimized network backbone. This can significantly improve upload speeds for geographically distant clients.
tips: Transfer Acceleration incurs additional per-GB charges.
The bucket name cannot contain dots when using acceleration.
Not all regions support Transfer Acceleration.
Advanced features read and change these settings in the bucket's own Region, and retry there when AWS redirects a request because your profile's default Region is different.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage patterns to optimize storage costs.

sections.heading: Configuring
sections.content: Set up Intelligent-Tiering configurations to automatically optimize storage costs based on object access patterns.
steps: Open Browse › More › Advanced features for the bucket.
Go to the Tiering tab.
Click Add Configuration.
Set a configuration ID and an optional prefix filter.
Configure the Archive Access and Deep Archive Access day thresholds.
Click Save.

sections.heading: Access Tiers
sections.content: Frequent Access (default). Infrequent Access (objects not accessed for 30 days). Archive Instant Access (not accessed for 90 days). Archive Access (optional, configurable). Deep Archive Access (optional, configurable).
tips: No retrieval fees for Intelligent-Tiering.
Small monitoring and automation fee per object.
Best for data with unknown or changing access patterns.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Server access logging records all requests made to your bucket and delivers log files to a target bucket.

sections.heading: Enabling Logging
sections.content: Enable server access logging to capture detailed records of all requests made to your bucket.
steps: Open Browse › More › Advanced features for the bucket.
Go to the Logging tab and choose Enable.
Enter the target bucket for log delivery.
Set an optional prefix for log files.
Optionally tick Grant the S3 logging service permission to write to the target bucket.
Save.
tips: The target bucket must be in the same region as the source bucket.

The delivery permission is opt-in. When ticked, Buckets reads the target bucket policy and adds one statement (logging.s3.amazonaws.com may PutObject under the target prefix, only for logs from this bucket and account), keeping every existing statement; nothing is written if an equivalent statement already exists. Requests to the target carry ExpectedBucketOwner. A prefix containing *, ? or $ is refused for the grant (a policy would read them as wildcards or variables), and if logging then fails to turn on, the added statement is removed again.

If the target bucket grants the S3 Log Delivery group write access through its ACL, or its policy can't be read, Buckets explains why and leaves the policy unchanged; add the shown statement yourself if needed.
Do not set the target bucket as the same bucket to avoid log loops.
Logs are delivered on a best-effort basis with some delay.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Object Lock prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a fixed amount of time or indefinitely. Used for regulatory compliance and data protection.

sections.heading: Legal Hold
sections.content: A legal hold prevents an object version from being deleted regardless of retention settings. It remains until explicitly removed.
steps: Select an object.
Open the Object Lock settings.
Toggle Legal Hold to On.
Click Save.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.content: Set a retention period with a mode: Governance mode (users with special permissions can override), Compliance mode (no one can delete until the period expires, including the root user).
tips: Object Lock must be enabled when creating the bucket.
Compliance mode retention cannot be shortened once set.
Legal holds and retention operate independently.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: With Requester Pays enabled, the person downloading data pays for requests and transfer instead of the bucket owner. Configure it in Browse › More › Advanced features › Requester Pays.

sections.heading: Effects
sections.content: S3 rejects requests that do not include the requester-pays header, so anonymous downloads stop working. To work with such a bucket from Buckets, choose Accept requester charges in Buckets; the consent lasts for this session only and resets when the setting changes, you sign out or the app restarts.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Bucket tags label a bucket for cost allocation and organisation. Edit them in Browse › More › Advanced features › Bucket tags.

sections.heading: Editing Tags
sections.content: Add or change key/value rows, then Save Tags. Saving with no keys removes all bucket tags. Tags used for per-bucket billed costs must also be activated as cost-allocation tags in the AWS Billing console.
tips: Object tags are separate — see Object Tagging.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The local index copies an S3 Inventory report into a database on this computer so you can search millions of objects instantly without listing the bucket. Configure it in Bucket settings › Local index; search it with Inventory index search (Browse › More › Inventory index).

sections.heading: Building the Index
sections.content: Choose the bucket's inventory configuration and Refresh now. Buckets reads the newest CSV or Parquet manifest (ORC reports can be queried in Athena instead) and shows progress by files, bytes and rows. AWS writes the first inventory report within about 24 hours of creating the configuration.
tips: Clear local index removes cached rows only — S3 objects and run history stay.
The last 25 refresh runs are listed with their status and duration.

sections.heading: Searching
sections.content: Inventory index search uses the same filter syntax as the object filter bar, across the whole bucket. Results page 100 at a time and can be sorted by key, size or modified date. Click a result to open it in Browse.

sections.heading: Live S3 Metadata
sections.content: If S3 Metadata tables are available in your region, you can enable them from the same tab after acknowledging the recurring cost, then search live inventory in Athena once AWS reports the table.

sections.heading: Annotation Table
sections.content: S3 Metadata can also maintain an annotation table with one row per object annotation (AWS-only). When enabling live metadata, tick Also create the annotation table. On a bucket that already has live metadata, the Annotation table card shows its state, role and errors; enter the IAM role S3 uses to manage the table and choose Enable annotation table. After the cost and permission review, Buckets calls UpdateBucketMetadataAnnotationTableConfiguration. Once AWS reports the table, Query annotations in Athena and Recent annotation changes (from the journal table) open prefilled queries in the Athena workbench. Disable annotation table asks for confirmation and does not delete any annotations.
tips: Recurring charges: S3 Tables storage and maintenance for the table, plus Athena bytes scanned per query.
Supplying a role also requires iam:PassRole on that role.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Every S3 object has associated metadata including system-defined headers and custom user-defined key-value pairs.

sections.heading: System Metadata
sections.content: Content-Type (MIME type, e.g. image/png). Content-Disposition (how the browser handles the file). Cache-Control (caching directives). Content-Encoding (compression encoding). Content-Language (language of the content).

sections.heading: Custom Metadata
sections.content: Add your own key-value pairs to objects for application-specific data or organizational purposes.
steps: Click the More menu on an object row.
Select "View Metadata".
View existing system and custom metadata.
Click "Add" to create a new custom key-value pair.
Edit existing values as needed.
Click Save to persist changes.
tips: Custom metadata keys are prefixed with x-amz-meta- automatically.
Metadata is limited to 2KB total size.
Changing metadata creates a copy of the object with the new metadata.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Tags are key-value pairs that help you categorize and manage your S3 objects. Tags can be used for access control, lifecycle rules, analytics, and cost allocation.

sections.heading: Managing Tags
sections.content: Add, edit, and remove tags on your S3 objects to organize and control access to your data.
steps: Click the More menu on an object row.
Select "View Tags".
View existing tags.
Click "Add Tag" to create a new key-value pair.
To remove a tag, click the delete button next to it.
Click Save to persist changes.

sections.heading: Use Cases
sections.content: Lifecycle rules can filter by tags. IAM policies can grant access based on tags. Cost allocation reports can group by tags. Analytics can segment by tags.
tips: Maximum 10 tags per object.
Tag keys must be unique within an object.
Tags do not affect object data, only metadata.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: S3 offers multiple storage classes optimized for different access patterns and cost requirements.

sections.heading: Available Storage Classes
sections.content: Standard: General purpose, default class. Standard-IA: Infrequent access, lower cost per GB, higher retrieval cost. One Zone-IA: Single availability zone, even lower cost. Glacier Instant Retrieval: Archive with millisecond access. Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Archive with minutes to hours retrieval. Deep Archive: Lowest cost with 12+ hour retrieval. Intelligent-Tiering: Automatic cost optimization.

sections.heading: Changing Storage Class
sections.content: Change the storage class of an object to optimize costs based on your access patterns.
steps: Click the More menu on an object row.
Select "Storage Class".
Select the desired storage class.
Confirm the change.
A lifecycle rule is created to transition the object.
tips: Minimum storage duration charges apply (30 days for IA, 90 days for Glacier).
Retrieval fees apply for IA and Glacier classes.
Use lifecycle rules for automated transitions of many objects.

sections.heading: Storage Class Analyzer
sections.content: Storage Class (bucket … menu › Storage Class, or "Storage Class" in the command palette) opens on the Analyzer tab: a breakdown of current objects by storage class with exact counts, bytes and percentages. Each run scans up to 10,000 current objects, clearly marks partial results, and does not change anything. Switch to the Bulk transition tab to move every object to a new class.

sections.heading: Bulk Transition and Tags
sections.content: Bulk transition asks you to review the cost first, then rewrites each object in place with CopyObject, asking S3 to copy its tags. Because tags can still be lost (missing tagging permissions or provider support), Buckets reads each object's tags before the copy and checks them again afterwards. Objects whose tags differ are listed, and Re-apply saved tags writes the saved tag sets back after a confirmation. It reads each object's current tags first and leaves alone any object whose tags were edited, or that was replaced, after the transition. This costs one extra GetObjectTagging request per object, plus a second one for objects that had tags.
tips: Saved tags are kept in memory for up to 5,000 objects per run and for the last 5 runs, and can only be re-applied with the same AWS profile; they are lost when the app quits.
Objects larger than 5 GB are skipped, and each rewrite resets the object's last-modified time.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Glacier Deep Archive and the Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers must be restored before they can be read. Glacier Instant Retrieval needs no restore.

sections.heading: Finding Archived Objects
sections.content: Glacier Restore (Browse › More › Glacier Restore, or the command palette) lists the archived files on the current Browse page. Choosing one opens the restore review — nothing is requested until you confirm. You can also use Restore from Glacier in an object's More actions menu.

sections.heading: Restore Tiers and Days
sections.content: Bulk is cheapest (about 5–12 hours, ~48 hours for Deep Archive), Standard is the default (3–5 hours, ~12 hours for Deep Archive), and Expedited is fastest (1–5 minutes) but not available for Deep Archive or Intelligent-Tiering. For Glacier classes choose how many days (1–365, default 7) the temporary copy stays available; it is billed at S3 Standard rates for that time.

sections.heading: Bulk Restore
sections.content: Select several archived files and choose Restore (n). Requests run eight at a time and the result lists initiated, extended and failed objects.

sections.heading: Restore Status
sections.content: The preview and restore dialog show whether a restore is in progress (refreshed every 30 seconds), complete with its expiry time, or not needed. Restoring an already-restored object extends its availability.
tips: Every restore shows a cost review with the object count, tier and duration first.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Generate ready-to-use code snippets for common S3 operations in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, Java, Rust, or C#. Code is pre-configured with your bucket and object context, so you can copy and paste it directly into your project with minimal modification.

sections.heading: Supported Languages
sections.content: Buckets generates code in seven popular languages, each using the recommended AWS SDK for that ecosystem.
tips: TypeScript (AWS SDK v3)
JavaScript (AWS SDK v3)
Python (boto3)
Go (AWS SDK for Go v2)
Java (AWS SDK for Java v2)
Rust (AWS SDK for Rust)
C# (AWS SDK for .NET)

sections.heading: Available Operations
sections.content: The following S3 operations are available for code generation: listBucketObjects, getObject, putObject, deleteObject, copyObject, getObjectUrl (presigned), createBucket, deleteBucket, getBucketPolicy, putBucketPolicy, and deleteBucketPolicy. Each operation generates a complete, runnable code snippet with proper error handling. In every language, getObject downloads to a local file, putObject uploads a local file, and deleteBucket includes an empty-bucket helper whose call is commented out, so nothing but the bucket itself is deleted unless you enable it. The Go, Java, Rust and C# snippets also include a deleteObjects helper that sends DeleteObjects with up to 1,000 keys per request, and their empty-bucket helper pages through the whole listing; the TypeScript, JavaScript and Python empty-bucket helpers delete only the first page of the listing (up to 1,000 objects), one object at a time.

sections.heading: How to Use
sections.content: Code generation is accessible from multiple places in the app, making it easy to generate snippets in the context of your current workflow.
steps: Right-click a bucket in the sidebar and select "Generate Code", or use the code generation button from the object list.
Select your preferred programming language.
Choose the S3 operation you need.
Review the generated code with syntax highlighting.
Click Copy to copy the code to your clipboard.
tips: Generated code includes all necessary imports and AWS SDK setup.
Credentials are not embedded in generated code for security.
You can modify the code before copying.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Execute generated snippets in all seven supported languages directly within Buckets. AWS credentials are injected only for the run step and are redacted from captured output.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.content: JavaScript and transpiled TypeScript run in the restricted Node.js VM, while Python uses the bundled runtime. Go, Java, Rust, and C# build and run in isolated temporary workspaces using their installed system toolchains; the workspace is removed after execution.

sections.heading: Running Code
sections.content: The code execution tool provides a full editor with syntax highlighting and an output panel for results.
steps: Open the Code Execution tool.
Write or paste your code in the editor.
Click Run to execute.
View the output in the results panel.
Errors and console output are captured and displayed.

sections.heading: Whitelisted Modules
sections.content: The following modules are available for import in the sandboxed environment: @aws-sdk/client-s3, @aws-sdk/lib-storage, @aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner, console, util, stream, buffer, and crypto. Any attempt to import modules outside this list will be blocked.

sections.heading: Security
sections.content: Credentials are automatically injected but sanitized from output. Access keys and secrets are redacted, output is size-limited, and execution time is capped. Compiled languages require the corresponding local toolchain and may take longer on their first run while SDK packages are restored.
tips: Your AWS credentials are automatically available in the execution context.
Use this to test S3 operations before using them in your application.
Output is limited and credentials are redacted for security.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Execute AWS CLI commands directly from Buckets with auto-injected credentials. No need to configure the CLI separately or manage credential files on your system.

sections.heading: Command Templates
sections.content: Buckets provides pre-built templates for common operations so you can get started quickly without memorizing CLI syntax.
tips: aws s3 ls — List buckets and objects
aws s3 cp — Copy files to and from S3
aws s3 sync — Sync directories with S3
aws s3api — Low-level API calls for advanced operations
aws s3 presign — Generate presigned URLs

sections.heading: Using the CLI
sections.content: The CLI tool provides a terminal-like experience within the app, complete with output display and command history.
steps: Open the CLI tool from the sidebar or tools menu.
Select a command template or type your own command.
Credentials are automatically set as environment variables.
Click Run to execute the command.
View the output in the terminal-like display.

sections.heading: Command History
sections.content: Previously executed commands are saved and can be re-run with a single click. Use the history to quickly repeat common operations without retyping commands.
tips: Commands run with your current profile's credentials.
The bundled AWS CLI is used, so no local installation is needed.
Use s3api for operations not available in the high-level s3 commands.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Export your bucket configuration as Infrastructure as Code templates. This is useful for replicating bucket setups across environments or for version-controlled infrastructure management.

sections.heading: Supported Formats
sections.content: Buckets supports exporting to all major IaC formats used in the AWS ecosystem.
tips: CloudFormation (YAML) — AWS native infrastructure template format
Terraform (HCL) — HashiCorp's multi-cloud infrastructure tool
AWS CDK (TypeScript) — Programmatic infrastructure with TypeScript
AWS CDK (Python) — Programmatic infrastructure with Python
SAM (YAML) — Serverless Application Model for Lambda-integrated setups

sections.heading: How to Export
sections.content: Exporting your bucket configuration is straightforward and produces ready-to-use templates.
steps: Open the IaC Export tool for a bucket.
Select the output format (CloudFormation, Terraform, CDK, or SAM).
Review the generated template with syntax highlighting.
Click Copy to copy the template to your clipboard.
tips: Templates include the bucket's current configuration.
You may need to adjust resource names and parameters for your environment.
CDK templates require the AWS CDK toolkit to deploy.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Query the contents of S3 objects using SQL expressions. Works with CSV, JSON, and Parquet files. S3 Select only retrieves the data you need, reducing data transfer and cost compared to downloading entire objects.

sections.heading: AWS Service Availability
sections.content: AWS closed S3 Select to new customers on July 25, 2024. Existing S3 Select customers can continue using it. A MethodNotAllowed response may indicate this restriction, but does not confirm account eligibility. Buckets preserves the service code and response and shows guidance in the query dialog. An IAM permission change cannot enable a service availability restriction. Use an account with existing access to test S3 Select, use Athena, or download the object for local analysis. S3-compatible provider support depends on the provider.

sections.heading: Supported Formats
sections.content: S3 Select works with three common data formats, each with configurable parsing options.
tips: CSV — Comma or custom-delimited files
JSON — Standard and JSON Lines format
Parquet — Columnar storage format

Compression — None, GZIP or BZIP2 for CSV and JSON, filled in automatically from the object's Content-Encoding or a .gz/.gzip/.bz2 key suffix. Parquet handles compression internally, so the control does not apply to it.

sections.heading: Running a Query
sections.content: The S3 Select tool provides a complete SQL editor with format configuration and output options.
steps: Open the S3 Select tool for an object.
Select the input format (CSV, JSON, or Parquet).
Configure format options (delimiter, headers, etc.).
Write your SQL query in the editor.
Select the output format (CSV or JSON).
Click Run Query.
View results in the output panel.

sections.heading: SQL Syntax
sections.content: S3 Select supports a subset of SQL: SELECT with column references or *, FROM S3Object, WHERE with comparison and logical operators, and LIMIT to restrict the number of rows returned. This covers the majority of data exploration and extraction use cases.
tips: S3 Select only scans the data needed, so it's cost-effective.
Use LIMIT to preview data before running full queries.
Parquet files work best due to their columnar format.
Results are capped at 10 MB; when the cap is hit, a Results truncated notice says only the first 10 MB are shown.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Compare the contents of two S3 objects side by side with a visual diff view. This is useful for tracking changes between file versions or comparing configurations across environments.

sections.heading: Using the Diff Tool
sections.content: The diff tool provides a clear visual comparison between any two S3 objects.
steps: Open the S3 Diff tool.
Select the first object (source).
Select the second object (target).
Click Compare.
View the diff with color-coded changes.

sections.heading: Diff Display
sections.content: Added lines are highlighted in green. Removed lines are highlighted in red. Unchanged lines are shown in gray. Line numbers are displayed for easy reference, making it straightforward to identify exactly what changed between two files. The two panes scroll together, both vertically and horizontally.
tips: Works best with text-based files.
Uses LCS algorithm for accurate diff calculation.
Useful for comparing config files or code between versions.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Generate various URL and identifier formats for S3 objects. Quickly get the exact format you need for your application, documentation, or IAM policies.

sections.heading: Available Formats
sections.content: The URI Builder generates all common S3 addressing formats in one place.
tips: S3 URI: s3://bucket-name/key (used in AWS CLI and SDKs)
ARN: arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/key (used in IAM policies)
HTTPS Path-Style: https://s3.region.amazonaws.com/bucket/key
HTTPS Virtual-Hosted: https://bucket.s3.region.amazonaws.com/key
ARNs and hosts follow the Region's partition: arn:aws with amazonaws.com, arn:aws-cn with amazonaws.com.cn for China Regions, and arn:aws-us-gov for AWS GovCloud (US).

sections.heading: How to Use
sections.content: The URI Builder is available for any object in your buckets and provides instant access to all URL formats.
steps: Open the URI Builder for an object.
View all generated URL formats.
Click Copy next to any format to copy it.
Customize parameters like account ID or region if needed.
tips: Path-style URLs are deprecated for new buckets; prefer virtual-hosted.
ARN format is required for IAM policies.
S3 URI format is used with aws s3 CLI commands.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The Athena Workbench runs SQL over data in S3 with Amazon Athena. Open it from Browse › More › Athena query (prefilled with the current bucket and folder) or the command palette, which can open any of its three tabs directly.

sections.heading: Query Editor
sections.content: Write SQL and Run. The status badge follows the query through Queued, Running and Succeeded or Failed, and you can Cancel at any time. After a run Buckets shows the bytes scanned with an estimate at $5 per TB (10 MB minimum) and flags partition improvements for large scans. Results load 1,000 rows at a time; rows can be copied.
tips: Save queries by name in the side list; they are stored per AWS profile on this device.

Each run shows a cost review first because Athena bills by data scanned. The exact bytes can't be known before Athena plans and runs the query, so the review states Athena's 10 MB minimum billable scan; the bytes actually scanned and their cost appear while and after the query runs.

sections.heading: History
sections.content: The History tab lists recent queries in the selected workgroup with their status, submission time, data scanned, run time and SQL (with the catalog and database). Edit copies a query into the editor; Run runs it again through the same cost review. Refresh reloads the list.

sections.heading: Glue Catalog
sections.content: Browse Glue databases and tables, see columns, partition keys and locations, and insert ready-made SELECT statements. Create table from S3 prefix builds a Glue table for Parquet, JSON, CSV, TSV or ORC data, with header and delimiter options for text formats. Optional partition keys must differ from the data columns; after creating a partitioned table, load its partitions with MSCK REPAIR TABLE or ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION. Text formats also take a compression setting: Auto, None, GZIP or BZIP2. Auto lists one page (up to 100 keys) under the location and decides from .gz/.bz2 suffixes, then checks Content-Encoding with HeadObject on up to 3 files if the suffixes don't decide it.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.content: Choose the workgroup, the S3 location for query results (locked when the workgroup enforces one), and the default database and catalog. The catalog picker lists the Region's Athena data catalogs; choose Other catalog… to type a name, which is also offered when the list can't be loaded. A query cannot run until a result location is available. Settings are saved per AWS profile.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Browse › More › Developer tools opens a launcher for four tools that work on the selected bucket: Diff Tool (compare objects or buckets), Lambda Builder, Two-Pane Compare & Sync, and S3 URI Builder.

sections.heading: Opening a Tool Directly
sections.content: Every tool — and both Diff Tool tabs — is also a command palette entry, so you can open, for example, Bucket diff without going through the launcher.
tips: Press Cmd+K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) and search for "Bucket diff", "Lambda Builder", "Two-Pane" or "URI Builder".

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Buckets integrates with Amazon CloudFront to help you manage CDN distributions alongside your S3 buckets. View, create, and manage distributions without leaving the app.

sections.heading: Switching to CloudFront View
sections.content: The CloudFront view is accessible from the sidebar view mode selector, giving you a dedicated panel for distribution management.
steps: In the sidebar, click the view mode selector.
Switch from "Storage (S3)" to "CloudFront".
The main panel now shows your CloudFront distributions.
Click any distribution to view its details.

sections.heading: Distribution List
sections.content: The list shows Distribution ID, Domain Name, Status (Deployed/InProgress), State (Enabled/Disabled), and Comment. You can copy the domain name to your clipboard with one click or open the distribution URL directly in your browser.

sections.heading: Origin Access Controls
sections.content: Open Operate → Open CloudFront → Origin Access Controls to list OACs for the active profile across all regions. This manager is available even when there are no distributions. Existing OACs show their ID, name, description, origin type, and signing settings.
steps: Enter a unique OAC name (1–64 characters) and an optional description, then select Create OAC. New standalone OACs use S3, always signing, and SigV4; they are not automatically attached to a distribution.
Use Refresh OACs to see AWS-side changes. A failed refresh displays an error rather than claiming that the account has no OACs.
To remove a disposable OAC, select Delete on its row, review its name, ID, and profile, then confirm Delete OAC. The app retrieves the current version before deleting.
tips: AWS rejects deletion while any distribution origin uses the OAC. The manager explains this error and does not detach origins or change distributions or bucket policies.

Required permissions: cloudfront:ListOriginAccessControls, cloudfront:CreateOriginAccessControl, cloudfront:GetOriginAccessControl, and cloudfront:DeleteOriginAccessControl. Profile read-only guardrails still apply to writes.
After an ambiguous create failure, refresh before retrying to check whether AWS created the OAC. Successful creation and a later refresh failure are reported separately.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Create a new CloudFront distribution to serve your S3 content through a global CDN for faster delivery and lower latency to users worldwide.

sections.heading: Creating a Distribution
sections.content: The distribution creation wizard guides you through selecting an origin and configuring basic settings.
steps: Switch to CloudFront view mode.
Click Create Distribution.
Select an S3 bucket as the origin.
Configure default behavior settings.
Add an optional comment or name.
Choose whether to enable the distribution immediately.
Click Create.

sections.heading: Origin Settings
sections.content: Select which S3 bucket to use as the content source. The bucket's region is automatically detected, and the origin domain name is configured for you.
tips: Distribution deployment takes 5-15 minutes.
You can create distributions for any bucket in your account.
Use custom domain names with SSL certificates for production.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Edit, update, and manage your existing CloudFront distributions directly from Buckets. All common distribution management tasks are available without switching to the AWS Console.

sections.heading: Available Actions
sections.content: Buckets supports the full lifecycle of distribution management: edit distribution settings, enable or disable a distribution, delete a distribution (must be disabled first), and create cache invalidations to clear cached content.

sections.heading: Cache Invalidation
sections.content: Cache invalidation forces CloudFront to fetch fresh content from your S3 origin, ensuring users see the latest version of your files.
steps: Select a distribution.
Click Create Invalidation.
Enter the paths to invalidate (e.g., /* for all content or /images/* for a specific folder).
Click Create.
The invalidation processes across all edge locations.
tips: You must disable a distribution before deleting it.
Cache invalidations take a few minutes to propagate globally.
The first 1,000 invalidation paths per month are free.

sections.heading: Configuration & History
sections.content: Manage › Configuration & history shows the distribution's full configuration as JSON and its invalidation history. Edits are protected by the configuration's ETag: review the changes, then confirm the update.

sections.heading: Specialist Controls
sections.content: The same dialog includes specialist controls: attach cache, origin-request, response-headers, real-time log, field-level encryption and continuous-deployment policies or a WAF web ACL; create reusable policy resources from JSON templates; and promote a staging distribution's configuration. Each change is reviewed before it is applied.
tips: Per-distribution actions need you to choose a distribution, so the command palette opens CloudFront and points you to the row's Manage menu.

sections.heading: S3 Site Doctor
sections.content: Manage › S3 site doctor checks a distribution's S3 origins for the usual causes of 403s and wrong pages: legacy Origin Access Identity, anonymous REST or public website-endpoint origins (versus Origin Access Control), a bucket policy that grants cloudfront.amazonaws.com scoped by AWS:SourceArn to this distribution, Block Public Access, the default root object, single-page-app routing (403 and 404 → /index.html with status 200), folder URLs (foo/ → foo/index.html), HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects and compression. Each finding with a fix has Review fix, which shows every field that changes (before and after), the IAM actions needed and any caveats.
steps: Open CloudFront, choose Manage on the distribution's row, then S3 site doctor.
Review the findings; problems and warnings are listed first.
Choose Review fix, check the changes, tick the confirmation and choose Apply fix.
The doctor runs again so you can confirm the result. CloudFront deploys distribution changes in a few minutes.
tips: Fixes are rebuilt from fresh AWS state and applied with the previewed distribution ETag (If-Match). If the distribution or bucket policy changed after the preview, nothing is changed and you are asked to run the doctor again.

Bucket-policy fixes append one statement and keep every existing statement. Statements that grant CloudFront without a SourceArn are reported but never edited, because other distributions may rely on them.

Moving an origin to OAC reuses an existing S3 OAC when one exists, updates the bucket policy before the distribution, and leaves any OAI or public-read grant in place for you to remove after verifying.

The folder index fix creates, tests and publishes a CloudFront Function and attaches it to the default behavior's viewer-request event (after a cost review). It is not offered when a viewer-request function or Lambda@Edge association already exists.
Per-profile read-only mode blocks applying fixes; diagnosis is read-only.

sections.heading: Flat-Rate Plan Advisor
sections.content: Manage › Flat-rate plan advisor compares the distribution's last 30 days of CloudWatch traffic (Requests and BytesDownloaded, us-east-1) with CloudFront's flat-rate plans (Free $0, Pro $15, Business $200 and Premium $1,000 per month, with 1M, 10M, 125M and 500M requests and 100 GB, 50 TB, 50 TB and 50 TB of transfer, listed with no overage charges) and an estimated pay-as-you-go bill. It shows how much of each allowance the traffic uses, which plans fit, and feature caveats such as Free having no logging or origin failover requiring Premium.
tips: AWS exposes no API for a distribution's current pricing plan, so the advisor never claims to know it. Check the CloudFront console.

Pay-as-you-go figures are estimates using United States, Mexico & Canada rates with every request priced as HTTPS; the range shows the account-wide always-free tier applied or already used. Plan and price data were captured from the CloudFront pricing page on 13 Oct 2026.
Requires cloudfront:GetDistribution and cloudwatch:GetMetricData. The analysis runs only when you choose Analyze.

sections.heading: CloudFront URLs for Objects
sections.content: When a bucket is an origin of a distribution, Browse adds More actions › Copy CloudFront URL to each file and the Inspector lists every CloudFront URL for the selected object. Origin paths, cache-behavior routing and alternate domain names are taken into account.

commands.title: S3 site doctor (OAC, SPA routing, index.html)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Build, test, deploy, and monitor AWS Lambda functions that react to objects in a bucket without leaving Buckets. The builder supports Node.js 20, 22, and 24 and Python 3.12 and 3.14 on x86_64 or arm64. It writes the handler, bundles its dependencies, scopes the IAM role to the bucket, connects the trigger, and then shows the function's logs and metrics.

sections.heading: Builder Steps
sections.content: Step 1, Configure: function name, runtime, memory (128 MB to 10,240 MB), timeout, Powertools, AWS X-Ray active tracing (on by default; X-Ray traces are billed separately), and Advanced settings. Step 2, Events: the S3 events, prefix and suffix filters, and how events are delivered (direct S3 notification, EventBridge rule, or SQS buffer). Step 3, Code: edit the handler in a code editor with S3-aware autocompletion and inline syntax errors, declare dependencies, and export CDK, SAM, or CloudFormation. Step 4, Simulate: run the handler locally against a generated or saved S3 event, optionally with the real object from the bucket. Step 5, Deploy: review permissions and recursion safety, deploy with live progress, then monitor and backfill.

sections.heading: Dependencies
sections.content: List npm packages (one per line, or paste a package.json) or a Python requirements.txt in the Dependencies tab. At deploy, packages are installed for Linux on the function's architecture: npm install with --os=linux and the matching --cpu for Node.js, and pip install of manylinux wheels for Python. The AWS SDK v3, boto3, and Powertools (from the managed layer) are skipped because the runtime provides them. The tab flags imports in the code that aren't declared. TypeScript handlers are compiled with the TypeScript compiler.
tips: Bundling needs npm (installed with Node.js) or Python 3 with pip on this computer.
Python packages must publish Linux wheels. Build others in CI and upload a ZIP.
Packages over 50 MB zipped are rejected. Move large dependencies into a layer.

sections.heading: Trigger Delivery
sections.content: Direct S3 notification invokes the function asynchronously and suits simple pipelines. EventBridge turns on EventBridge delivery for the bucket and creates a rule that matches the bucket, events, and key filters, so several consumers can process the same objects without notification conflicts (replication events are not available). SQS buffer creates an encrypted queue with a dead-letter queue (or uses an SQS failure destination you supply), points the bucket at it, and polls it in batches, so bursts and rate-limited downstream systems are handled with per-message retries. For EventBridge and SQS, Buckets packages a small adapter so the handler still receives the event.Records[].s3 shape.

sections.heading: Advanced Settings
sections.content: Advanced settings on the Configure step cover architecture (arm64 costs about 20% less), environment variables, ephemeral /tmp storage up to 10,240 MB, reserved concurrency, async retry attempts and maximum event age, an SQS or SNS failure destination, VPC subnets and security groups, up to four additional layers, and publishing a version with an alias. When an alias is set, the trigger targets the alias, so rolling back means pointing the alias at an earlier version.

sections.heading: Permissions and Recursion Safety
sections.content: The execution role is scoped to the trigger bucket. Choose Match the code (actions are inferred from the SDK calls in the handler), Read only, or Read & write, and add other actions such as s3tables:PutTableData. IAM and STS actions are refused. The policy document is shown before deploying. If a role created by Buckets is reused, its policy is updated, and the X-Ray write policy is attached only when tracing is on and the role doesn't already have it; other roles are left unchanged and the deploy lists what they need. Preflight blocks a deploy when the handler writes into the prefix it listens to, because each output would invoke it again. Set an output prefix outside the trigger prefix, or acknowledge the risk after handling it in code. Lambda recursive loop detection is also turned on.

sections.heading: Simulation
sections.content: Simulation runs the handler in an isolated local process without your AWS credentials. Presets cover single and multiple records, encoded keys, delete markers, and malformed events. Turn on Use the real object to have GetObject and HeadObject return the actual object at that key (up to 10 MB, read-only). Calls that would change data, such as PutObject, CopyObject, DeleteObject, or SQS SendMessage, are recorded and listed instead of being sent. Save payloads you reuse; they're kept on this device per function.

sections.heading: Deployment
sections.content: The sidebar lists the functions in the Region. Redeploy loads a function that has one trigger from this bucket (a direct S3 notification, the Buckets EventBridge rule or the Buckets SQS queue) back into the builder with its settings, trigger and existing role, so it goes through the normal preflight and review before deploying. A single handler file, or a Builder package with the EventBridge/SQS adapter, is loaded as editable code and rebuilt; any other package (dependencies, several modules) is redeployed exactly as deployed, and only its settings, permissions and trigger can be changed. The SQS queue and its mapping are updated in place. When a function can't be redeployed (container image, unsupported runtime, package over 50 MB, several triggers, or a rule or queue Buckets didn't create), the sidebar says why before you click. Review the AWS account, full IAM requirements, invocation permission, notification before/after configuration, trigger resources, and rollback plan before deploying. The five-minute review is bound to this configuration, session and captured AWS state; changes require a new review. Deployment records undo actions and attempts to restore captured state after a failure. The resource report identifies completed and failed rollback actions, exact resource identifiers and manual cleanup. Download the JSON report and verify AWS state before marking cleanup complete.
steps: Complete the builder steps and expand the IAM, notification, trigger/configuration and rollback sections on Deploy.
Resolve any trigger conflicts and recursion warnings.
Click Deploy to AWS and confirm the cost review.
Watch each step report progress: account, package, role, function, configuration, permission, and trigger.
Invoke a test event, then use Monitor and Process existing objects.
tips: Your credentials need Lambda and IAM permissions, plus EventBridge or SQS for those delivery modes.

Exports preserve the selected runtime and reference the existing bucket. Install the displayed dependencies for CDK/SAM; raw CloudFormation requires a compiled handler ZIP in CodeS3Bucket/CodeS3Key. EventBridge/SQS and advanced deployment settings still require the Buckets workflow; exports use a direct S3 trigger.
Exported stacks preserve unrelated notification routes and remove their own route on deletion. Review retained CloudWatch logs and deployment artifacts separately.

sections.heading: Rehearse Rollback Locally
sections.content: On Deploy, choose Rehearse late-stage rollback locally to run the real deployment transaction against simulated resources and fail after trigger setup. Rehearse cleanup failure locally also denies function deletion, so the report shows the retained function and role requiring cleanup. Both controls make no AWS calls, use no AWS credentials and run no handler code. They test transaction/report behavior, not AWS permissions, propagation or installed-build acceptance. Malformed-event simulation tests the handler and is a separate check.

sections.heading: Monitor and Backfill
sections.content: After deploying, Monitor shows CloudWatch invocations, errors and error rate, throttles, average and p99 duration, and peak concurrency for 1 hour, 3 hours, 24 hours, or 7 days, plus a log viewer with time ranges, filter patterns, and a live tail that polls every 5 seconds. Triggers only fire for new uploads, so Process existing objects counts the matching objects already in the bucket and invokes the function asynchronously once per object (up to 100,000) with a synthetic ObjectCreated event, with progress and a Stop button.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: View and manage the Lambda functions triggered by S3 events on a bucket. Each function has Code, Settings, and Monitor views.

sections.heading: Viewing Triggers
sections.content: The trigger list shows the Lambda functions connected to a bucket's S3 event notifications.
steps: Open the Triggers Management modal for a bucket.
View all Lambda triggers configured for the bucket.
See function name, event types, and filter configurations.
Click a trigger to view its code, settings, and monitoring.

sections.heading: Editing Triggers
sections.content: Change a trigger's events and prefix or suffix filters. In Settings, edit the function's memory, timeout, /tmp storage, reserved concurrency, and environment variables, and see EventBridge rules and queue mappings that also invoke it. Single-file functions can be edited and redeployed from the Code view; only the code changes, so environment, layers, tracing, and VPC settings are kept. Functions with dependencies or several files are read-only here and are redeployed from Lambda Builder so nothing is dropped.

sections.heading: Deleting Triggers
sections.content: Remove triggers that are no longer needed to clean up your event notification configuration.
steps: Open the Triggers Management modal.
Find the trigger you want to remove.
Click Delete.
Confirm the removal.
The S3 event notification is removed.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Configure an S3 bucket to host a static website. Buckets guides you through the setup, including bucket policy configuration for public access, so you can get your site online quickly.

sections.heading: Setting Up
sections.content: Buckets walks you through each step of enabling static website hosting on a bucket.
steps: Create a new bucket with Static Website Hosting enabled, or open settings for an existing bucket.
Configure the index document (usually index.html).
Optionally set an error document (e.g., 404.html).
The app automatically generates the required bucket policy for public access.
Upload your website files to the bucket.
Access your site at the provided website URL.

sections.heading: Website URL
sections.content: Your website is accessible at http://bucket-name.s3-website-region.amazonaws.com. You can copy the URL from the guide modal. For custom domains, use CloudFront with an SSL certificate for HTTPS support.
tips: Static website hosting only supports HTTP, not HTTPS.
For HTTPS, use CloudFront in front of the S3 website endpoint.
Remember to disable Block Public Access for the bucket.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Browse local and S3 folders side by side, or compare two S3 locations. Run a bounded recursive dry-run before applying a locked update or mirror plan. S3-to-S3 workspaces support different prefixes, buckets, and AWS Regions.

sections.heading: Review Before Applying
sections.content: Dry-run compare lists up to 10,000 objects per side and classifies left-only, right-only, matching, newer, and ambiguous paths. A capped result is review-only: the app will not turn an incomplete inventory into a sync selection.
steps: Open Two-Pane Compare & Sync and choose a bucket and prefix on each side.
Run Dry-run compare and approve the regional S3 LIST cost and permission review.
Inspect the change preview and checksum confidence.
Select left-to-right or right-to-left changes, or manually select objects.
Choose Copy or Move and review the separate write-cost preflight.
For Move, acknowledge the destructive confirmation; source keys are deleted only after destination verification.

sections.heading: Local ↔ S3 Update and Mirror
sections.content: The left pane is the source for local/S3 synchronization. Update copies source-only and source-newer files while preserving target-only, target-newer, and ambiguous conflicts. Mirror treats the source as authoritative: it can overwrite conflicts and delete target-only files, so it adds a destructive confirmation. The plan is locked for 15 minutes; changed source files and changed remote deletion targets fail closed.
steps: Switch either pane to Local and choose a real folder. Symbolic links and special files are excluded.
Put the intended authoritative source on the left, then run Dry-run compare.
Optionally choose Verify content checksums. This downloads reviewed S3 objects within the displayed byte budget and computes SHA-256 locally.
Choose Apply update for a conservative merge, or Mirror target for authoritative-source semantics.
Review permissions, regional request/transfer estimates, copy counts, preserved conflicts, and mirror deletions before continuing.

sections.heading: Checksums, Limits, and Saved Workspaces
sections.content: Equal size and ETag is treated as a metadata match, never a universal content checksum. Local/S3 metadata matches use equal size and timestamps within two seconds; explicit SHA-256 verification is the content-confidence path. Encryption, multipart uploads, and compatible providers can change ETag semantics. Saved workspaces store only local paths, bucket names, and prefixes on this device and never store credentials.
tips: Cross-Region transfer, KMS, retrieval, request, and storage charges can apply.
Copy uses S3 server-side copy and multipart upload-copy for large objects; data is not downloaded through the desktop app.
Use S3 Replication for continuously managed replication rather than periodically repeating a manual workspace.

Deleting in a pane sends selected files in DeleteObjects batches of up to 1,000 keys and deletes selected folders recursively. Every result is checked, so the toast reports exactly how many items were deleted and how many failed, with the first error.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: View and manage multipart uploads in progress. Abort stuck or incomplete uploads to free up storage and avoid unnecessary costs from orphaned upload parts.

sections.heading: Managing Uploads
sections.content: The Multipart Upload Management tool gives you visibility into all active multipart uploads for a bucket.
steps: Open the Multipart Upload Management tool.
View all active multipart uploads for the bucket.
See upload ID, initiation date, and key for each.
Select an upload to view its parts.
Click Abort to cancel a stuck upload.

sections.heading: Why Abort Uploads
sections.content: Incomplete multipart uploads continue to incur storage costs for uploaded parts. If an upload was interrupted or failed, these parts remain until explicitly aborted or cleaned up by a lifecycle rule. Regularly reviewing and aborting incomplete uploads helps control costs.
tips: Set up lifecycle rules to automatically clean up incomplete uploads.
Each part of a multipart upload is stored separately until completion.
Aborting an upload deletes all uploaded parts.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Access points are named network endpoints with dedicated access policies that simplify managing data access at scale for shared S3 buckets. Each access point has its own permissions and network controls.

sections.heading: Creating an Access Point
sections.content: Create a new access point to provide a scoped entry point to your bucket with its own policy.
steps: Open the Access Points tool.
Click Create Access Point.
Enter a name for the access point.
Configure the access point policy (JSON).
Set network origin (Internet or VPC).
Click Create.

sections.heading: Managing Access Points
sections.content: View access point details including ARN and policy. Edit access point policies to adjust permissions. Delete access points that are no longer needed.
tips: Access points can restrict access to a VPC for enhanced security.
Each access point has its own DNS name.
Use access points to simplify bucket policies for multi-team buckets.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Perform large-scale batch operations on S3 objects. Process millions of objects with a single request, ideal for bulk tagging, copying, or invoking Lambda functions across large datasets.

sections.heading: Creating a Batch Job
sections.content: The Batch Operations tool walks you through creating and submitting a batch job.
steps: Open Browse › More › Advanced features and go to the Batch tab.
Configure the job (operation type, manifest, etc.).
Choose Review exact job to preview the manifest and cost.
Submit the job.
Monitor job progress and status.

sections.heading: Manifest Preview and Cost
sections.content: Review exact job reads the manifest before anything is created. It HEADs the manifest and checks its ETag against the one you entered; on a mismatch it offers Use current ETag. For a CSV manifest it counts the rows from the first 1 MiB and estimates the total beyond that, and shows sample keys; for an S3 Inventory manifest.json it lists the inventory data files. The cost estimate adds $0.25 per job, $1.00 per million objects processed, and the request cost of the chosen operation, at US East (N. Virginia) list prices reviewed on 2026-10-23; other Regions can differ slightly.

sections.heading: Monitoring Jobs
sections.content: View job status (Active, Preparing, Completing, Completed, or Failed). Track completion percentage in real time. List all batch jobs for your account to keep track of ongoing and historical operations.

sections.heading: Background Work at a Glance
sections.content: Automation Command Center shows separate counts for sync profiles with errors, transfers needing attention, and failed scan schedules. It also summarizes running work, paused transfers, automatic sync profiles, and scheduled scans, with links to Transfers, Folder Sync, Scans, and Safe Workflow Recipes.

sections.heading: Failure Visibility
sections.content: Transfer counts use the same grouped queue as the Transfers panel: the latest attempt for each transfer, plus folder moves, cross-bucket copies/moves, ZIP/folder downloads, and restores. An older failed attempt replaced by a newer retry is not counted again. Interrupted work appears under paused transfers, separate from failures; paused-only work shows Work paused. Single-file history is limited to the latest 100 retained journal records. Sync profiles and scan schedules contribute their latest status once, not totals from Folder Sync run history. Routine push approval pauses, successes, and intentional cancellations are not failures; large-deletion safety stops still mark the sync profile as an error. A failed status read is shown as unavailable, rather than Idle. Idle describes local application state, not AWS resource health.

sections.heading: Scheduler Boundary
sections.content: The dashboard does not create a durable cloud control plane. Scheduled scans and local watchers run while Buckets is open, missed due times are checked at the next start, and closing the application stops local scheduling. Use AWS-native services when execution must continue without the desktop app.

sections.heading: Credential-Free Handoffs
sections.content: Team Access Hub exports a small JSON handoff containing the saved account label, authentication method, Region, selected bucket, optional prefix, and a Buckets deep link. Access keys, secret keys, session tokens, private keys, and SSO tokens are never included.

sections.heading: No Implicit Access Grant
sections.content: A handoff is navigation context, not an invitation system and not an IAM grant. The recipient must configure their own authorized profile or SSO role. Opening a handoff preserves the normal account-switch and permission boundaries.

sections.heading: Safe Sharing
sections.content: Review the bucket and account label before sending a handoff. Treat bucket names and prefixes as potentially sensitive metadata even though the bundle contains no credentials. A handoff can be copied only after a bucket is selected.

sections.heading: Native Least-Privilege Access
sections.content: After an explicit permission-and-pricing review, the Operate workspace lists registered Access Grants locations and grants in the selected Region. Create IAM-user, IAM-role, Identity Center user, or Identity Center group grants with READ, WRITE, or READWRITE permission and an optional location-relative subprefix. A grant cannot create public access.

sections.heading: Prerequisites and Scope
sections.content: AWS permits one Access Grants instance per account and Region. Before creating a grant, register an S3 location and an assumable IAM role in AWS. Buckets intentionally does not invent the role trust policy or silently create an instance. Prefixes may target data that does not exist yet, while bucket-level targets must exist.

sections.heading: Test a Minimal Session
sections.content: Test 15-min session calls GetDataAccess with Minimal privilege. The result shows the matched grant and expiration, while access-key, secret-key, and session-token material is withheld from the renderer. The test proves grant matching; it does not convert the app's active profile or expose credentials for copying.

sections.heading: Deletion and Audit Boundary
sections.content: Deleting a grant prevents new sessions through that grant but cannot invalidate temporary credentials already issued; those remain usable until their expiry. Management calls and GetDataAccess are request-priced, pass through permission and live-pricing review, and are recorded by the app's audit trail and applicable AWS audit services.

sections.heading: What Is Protected
sections.content: Encrypted Vaults use a fresh random salt and IV with scrypt and AES-256-GCM. File bytes, filenames, timestamps, sizes, and the vault index are inside an authenticated encrypted payload before upload. S3 stores opaque UUID-named objects and an encrypted manifest; the password is held only while the dialog is open and is never persisted.

sections.heading: What Remains Visible
sections.content: AWS and anyone with bucket-list permission can still see that a .s3console-vault namespace exists, the number and byte size of encrypted S3 objects, update times, the vault ID metadata used for grouping, and request/access patterns. Object size includes small encryption overhead but is not padded. Bucket, prefix, account, Region, storage class, and AWS-side encryption settings remain visible.

sections.heading: No Password Recovery
sections.content: Buckets has no recovery key, escrow, password reset, or back door. Initialization requires a matching confirmation and at least 12 characters, but password strength and safekeeping remain the user's responsibility. Losing the password or corrupting the only manifest makes filenames and content unrecoverable; retain independent backups and version the bucket.

sections.heading: Safe Writes and Downloads
sections.content: Files are streamed into a permission-restricted encrypted temporary file, then uploaded under an opaque key. The manifest is conditionally replaced using its ETag so concurrent writers fail instead of losing entries; a failed manifest update triggers best-effort orphan cleanup. Downloads authenticate completely into a temporary destination before replacing the user-selected path. Symlinks, unsafe names, namespace escapes, duplicate entries, invalid sizes, oversized manifests, and modified ciphertext fail closed.

sections.heading: Connect a Compatible Endpoint
sections.content: From the Everything home screen, open S3-compatible, enter an endpoint origin, signing Region (or auto), access key, secret, and addressing style, then run Test & connect. The signed ListBuckets result becomes the active bucket list. The endpoint and credentials are saved through the same OS-backed encrypted credential store used for AWS access-key sessions and restored during explicit auto-login.

sections.heading: Provider Presets
sections.content: Presets build and validate the endpoint, signing Region, and addressing style from one or two values, using each provider's documented endpoint format. Hosted presets: Cloudflare R2 (account, EU, and FedRAMP jurisdictions; Account ID), Backblaze B2 (region), DigitalOcean Spaces (datacenter), Wasabi (region), Tigris (fixed t3.storage.dev), Hetzner (fsn1, nbg1, hel1), Scaleway (fr-par, nl-ams, pl-waw, it-mil), OVHcloud (region identifier such as gra or eu-west-par), IDrive e2 (the per-user endpoint and Region from your dashboard), Akamai/Linode (endpoint prefix such as us-southeast-1), Oracle OCI (namespace and region), Storj (hosted gateway), Google Cloud Storage (XML API with HMAC keys), and Supabase Storage (project ref and region, or a local API URL). Self-hosted presets take your server origin: MinIO, Garage (Region from s3_region, garage by default), Ceph RGW, SeaweedFS, and RustFS. Picking a self-hosted preset is remembered for that origin on this device so feature gating survives restarts.

sections.heading: Provider Capability Matrix
sections.content: Each preset carries a documented capability matrix for versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle, CORS, bucket policy, ACLs, object tagging, static website hosting, storage classes, presigned URLs, multipart upload, and flexible checksums, with links to the provider pages it comes from. The Test & connect preview shows the matrix, and reopening the dialog while connected shows the active provider. Features a provider documents as unsupported are disabled with a "Not supported by <provider>" tooltip or replaced by an explanation instead of failing with a provider error: Bucket Settings tabs, Access Control and permission tabs, object tagging, storage-class tools, presigned URLs, and the Object Lock, versioning, website, and Block Public Access switches when creating a bucket. AWS-only surfaces such as notifications, replication, inventory, CloudWatch metrics, Cost Explorer, IAM policy, and Block Public Access are disabled for every compatible connection. Features a provider does not document stay available with an Untested marker.

sections.heading: Checksum Compatibility
sections.content: Newer AWS SDKs add CRC32 flexible checksums to every upload by default, which providers such as Backblaze B2, Storj, and Supabase reject. Every compatible client in Buckets (browsing, the upload worker, saved-account transfers, and the connection test) uses requestChecksumCalculation and responseChecksumValidation set to WHEN_REQUIRED, and replaces the CRC32 header the SDK still adds to checksum-required operations such as DeleteObjects and bucket CORS or lifecycle writes with Content-MD5. A checksum algorithm you choose explicitly is never rewritten. Uploads set Content-Type from the file extension.

sections.heading: Compatibility Suite
sections.content: Maintainers run scripts/compat-suite.mjs against MinIO, Garage, and SeaweedFS containers from test/compat/docker-compose.yml, nightly in the s3-compat workflow. The suite builds clients with the same configuration as the app and exercises bucket create, put, get, head, list, copy, delete, batch delete, multipart upload, presigned GET, tagging, and versioning when the capability matrix marks it supported, then cleans up.

sections.heading: Transport and URL Safety
sections.content: Remote endpoints must use HTTPS. Plain HTTP is allowed only for localhost, 127.0.0.1, or ::1 development. Embedded usernames/passwords, URL paths (except Supabase Storage's fixed /storage/v1/s3 prefix), query strings, fragments, non-HTTP schemes, and invalid signing Regions are rejected in the main process before an S3 client is constructed. Connecting intentionally authorizes that endpoint to receive signed requests; verify the provider hostname and TLS ownership.

sections.heading: Supported Surface
sections.content: The shared core S3 client and background upload worker carry the custom endpoint and path-style setting, covering bucket/object browsing and the standard upload path. Region-redirect inference is disabled because compatible providers do not necessarily use AWS endpoint semantics. AWS-only surfaces—including CloudFront, Cost Explorer, Access Grants, S3 Tables, S3 Vectors, Bedrock, IAM, Lambda, Storage Lens, and Batch Operations—remain AWS-specific and can fail or be unavailable while a compatible endpoint is active.

sections.heading: Session Isolation and Pricing
sections.content: Changing credentials, endpoint, or addressing style destroys cached clients. Switching to AWS SSO or CLI explicitly clears the custom endpoint in both the main process and upload worker so signed AWS credentials cannot be sent to the prior provider. The preflight cannot infer a third-party contract, so provider request, storage, egress, and allowance costs are labelled usage-dependent rather than applying an AWS Region rate.

sections.heading: Two Explicit Cost Gates
sections.content: Plan index update first performs a bounded LIST-only inventory after regional permission and cost review. It accepts supported text/code extensions, at most 2 MiB per object, 250 MiB total, 5,000 candidate objects, and 100 pages. A capped plan is rejected by both the interface and main process; narrow the prefix. A second review shows the exact locked GET count and bytes before content is downloaded.

sections.heading: Local Keyed-Hash Index
sections.content: Downloaded text is normalized and split into unique words in the main process. Buckets stores object key, source size, ETag, index time, and HMAC-SHA256 token hashes in a local SQLite database. The random HMAC key is protected with Electron safeStorage when the operating system supports it. Plaintext content, snippets, embeddings, and search queries are not stored or sent to a cloud search service.

sections.heading: Search Semantics
sections.content: Search is exact normalized word matching with AND semantics: every entered word must occur in a result. It intentionally does not claim phrase, substring, fuzzy, stemming, semantic, or ranked relevance search. Filenames are not content matches. Unicode is NFKC-normalized and case-folded; duplicate words do not inflate a result.

sections.heading: Freshness, Failure, and Erasure
sections.content: Each GET is locked to the planned ETag. Modified objects fail instead of indexing unreviewed bytes. Successful objects replace their prior hashes transactionally; failed objects retain the older entry and are reported as stale. After a complete listing, objects no longer in scope are pruned. Clear local index removes this account-and-bucket's local metadata and hashes without calling or changing S3.

sections.heading: Privacy Boundary
sections.content: Keyed hashes make a copied database substantially harder to dictionary-attack without the local secret, but they are not encryption of the displayed object metadata. Bucket names, object keys, sizes, ETags, index times, word equality patterns, local search activity in memory, and S3 GET activity can still be observable to someone with the relevant local or AWS access. Use Encrypted Vaults when filenames themselves must be concealed.

sections.heading: Real Filesystem, Optional Prerequisite
sections.content: Virtual Drive launches the separately installed rclone mount command for the current bucket and prefix. macOS requires macFUSE, Windows requires WinFsp, and Linux requires FUSE 3. Buckets detects rclone on PATH but does not download, install, approve, or update rclone or kernel/filesystem drivers. A mount succeeds only after the operating system prerequisite accepts it. When something is missing, the dialog shows the Virtual drive setup guide with exact per-OS steps.

sections.heading: Read-Only Default
sections.content: Every new mount is read-only unless Allow writes and deletes is explicitly enabled and its open-ended permission/cost review is acknowledged. The mount target must be a real, empty, non-symlink local directory so existing local files cannot be shadowed. One mount is supported at a time; bucket and prefix delimiters/control characters are validated before the rclone remote argument is built.

sections.heading: Credentials and Companion Isolation
sections.content: The active access-key or temporary SSO session is passed to rclone through a minimized child environment, never command-line arguments. The child does not inherit arbitrary application environment variables or the user's rclone configuration. Custom S3-compatible endpoint and path-style settings are forwarded. Local processes with permission to inspect Buckets or its child can still access session credentials.

sections.heading: Write Cache and Clean Unmount
sections.content: Read-only mode disables the VFS content cache. Write mode uses rclone's writes cache and a five-second write-back delay, so plaintext pending writes exist in an app-private local cache until clean unmount; the cache directory is removed after a clean exit. If unmount times out or the process crashes, cache files are retained for recovery rather than silently discarded. Close files before unmounting.

sections.heading: S3 Is Not a POSIX Filesystem
