sections.content: Rclone translates file operations into S3 requests, but S3 does not provide native directories, random in-place writes, POSIX permissions, locks, atomic rename, or consistent behavior for every desktop application. Request totals, retrieval, KMS, storage, retries, multipart writes, and provider egress remain usage-dependent while mounted. For predictable bulk work, use Browse, Two-Pane Compare & Sync, or Folder Sync.

sections.heading: Quit Behavior
sections.content: A live mount is treated as an active operation. Quitting warns alongside uploads, downloads, and syncs; Close Anyway sends an interrupt and waits for clean unmount before exiting. Auto-update shutdown is time-bounded, so reopen the app and inspect the cache if the operating system forced an unclean exit.

sections.heading: Finder and Explorer Workflow
sections.content: Each Folder Sync profile can open its real local mirror directly in Finder, Windows Explorer, or the Linux file manager. Work with ordinary desktop files, then let the existing hash-aware sync engine preview and reconcile changes to the configured S3 prefix.

sections.heading: Safe Boundary
sections.content: Desktop Folder Bridge is not a FUSE, kernel, or virtual-drive mount and does not pretend S3 has filesystem semantics. Opening a folder sends no AWS request. Uploads, overwrites, and deletions occur only through Folder Sync, including its first-run dry preview and permission/cost review.

sections.heading: Edge Cases
sections.content: The main process verifies that the profile belongs to the active account, the path is absolute, and the resolved path still exists as a directory. Deleted folders and profiles from another account fail closed. Polling-mode warnings remain visible when the operating-system watcher limit prevents real-time detection.

sections.heading: Operational Posture
sections.content: The Security Control Center consolidates the active profile mutation gate, selected-bucket scan schedule, latest scan failure, and newly public-object delta. Critical and high findings receive an alert state; missing schedules are review items; informational profile state does not manufacture a security score.

sections.heading: Fail-Visible Findings
sections.content: A failed latest scan remains visible instead of being treated as clean. A temporary profile unlock is high severity until it expires. Newly public objects are critical. With no selected bucket, the center reports unknown bucket scope rather than claiming protection.

sections.heading: Authority Boundary
sections.content: This is a local Buckets operational view. It is not AWS Security Hub, GuardDuty, IAM Access Analyzer, Macie, CloudTrail, or a compliance certification. Scan schedules are bound to the verified AWS account/principal and named profile, run while the application is open and that profile is signed in, and retry overdue work after sign-in. Legacy schedules need explicit review and reconfiguration. Public-object deltas compare successful runs of the same schedule. Scheduled checks fail visibly when required reads are denied or the object limit prevents complete coverage. Security status refreshes every 15 seconds while Guardrails is open and can also be refreshed manually. Pausing remains available when AWS authentication fails. Authoritative AWS findings must be verified in their source services.

sections.heading: Guided Plans, Not Hidden Automation
sections.content: Recipes are local, non-executing checklists that connect a desired outcome to existing Buckets tools. Opening or checking a step never calls AWS. The destination tool retains its permission and regional cost preflight, configuration diff, production unlock, and destructive confirmation.

sections.heading: Included Recipes
sections.content: Start with Make a bucket recoverable, Lower storage cost safely, Collect files from an external partner, or Publish a private-origin website. Each step explains why it exists, labels its risk, and carries the active bucket only when the workflow supports that scope.

sections.heading: Failure and Scope Safety
sections.content: Bucket-required steps remain disabled until a bucket is selected. Checklist completion is a personal planning aid, not proof that AWS state changed. Return to the destination tool or AWS audit history to verify the actual resource state after every operation.
tips: A completed checkbox never substitutes for a recovery drill or live configuration read.
Cross-service workflows can partially succeed; inspect audit results before retrying.

commands.title: Recipe: Collect files from an external partner

sections.heading: Temporary Download Shares
sections.content: Generate a native S3 presigned download URL with an exact expiry of up to seven days and an optional recipient or purpose label. Share history is scoped to the active AWS account and stores metadata only—the bearer URL is never persisted. Anyone who possesses the URL can download until it expires.
tips: Copy the URL when it is generated; Share History cannot reveal it later.
Forgetting metadata removes only the local record and does not revoke the signed URL.
Native S3 presigned URLs cannot enforce a password, download count, or reliable per-link revocation. Use an authenticated application or CloudFront-backed gateway when those controls are mandatory.

sections.heading: Branded Upload Requests
sections.content: Upload Requests use Drop Zones: recipient-facing pages that submit directly to a dedicated S3 prefix without AWS credentials. Choose Minimal, Branded, or Friendly presentation, add a recipient note, and host the page or save it as HTML. S3 POST policy conditions enforce the destination prefix, per-file size, compatible single MIME prefix, and hard expiry.

sections.heading: Enforcement Boundaries
sections.content: Maximum file count and multi-pattern type presets are browser-page controls and can be bypassed by reopening or copying a page. Pausing removes tracked hosted pages and refuses new page generation, but previously saved local HTML remains usable until its signed policy expires. Pages signed with temporary SSO, STS or AWS CLI login credentials stop working when those credentials expire, which can be sooner than the selected request expiry; pages signed with long-lived IAM access keys stay valid until the zone expires. Logging out of Buckets does not revoke pages that were already generated. The page checks the expiry when it loads; an already-open page is not disabled at the expiry time, but S3 rejects uploads after it.
tips: Use a unique least-privilege prefix for each request.
Remove a hosted page or revoke the scoped DropZonesPublicRead statement when public access is no longer needed.
Under AWS CLI browser login, pages are signed with the session's resolved temporary credentials; if they can't be resolved, Buckets refuses to generate the page and asks you to sign in again.

Remove expired zones (older than 30 days) clears saved zones whose expiry passed more than 30 days ago. It removes only the saved settings; hosted page objects stay in S3 until you delete that zone on its own.
Inspect received objects before moving them into trusted workflows.

sections.heading: Choose a Safe Checkpoint
sections.content: Time Machine folds object versions and delete markers into the state that existed at an exact timestamp. Recent activity is grouped into one-hour change windows. Selecting a window travels to one millisecond before its earliest change, which is useful when you know approximately when an accidental overwrite or deletion began.
tips: Open Time Travel from Browse › More › Time Travel or the command palette. If versioning is off, Buckets explains that and opens Bucket Settings › Versioning; while the versioning status is still loading or could not be read, the menu item shows Checking or Unknown.
The timeline is scoped to the folder currently open in Time Travel.
Time Travel uses the selected Region and follows a valid bucket Region reported by AWS. A configured S3-compatible endpoint is retained.

Suspended versioning is warned in the browsing view and restore planner. Retained versions remain browsable, but overwritten or deleted null versions may be unrecoverable and snapshots may be incomplete. Re-enable versioning to retain future changes.
A truncated activity scan is labelled and must not be treated as a complete incident timeline.

sections.heading: Review the Difference
sections.content: The restore plan compares the chosen checkpoint with the current latest state. It separates historical versions that would be copied into new latest versions, currently-live keys that would receive delete markers, and unchanged keys. The exact reviewed key set is locked before execution, while the server recomputes live state to avoid restoring stale assumptions.

sections.heading: Run a Recovery Drill
sections.content: A recovery drill is read-only. It scans the full selected scope and uses HeadObject against a sample of up to 20 historical version IDs to prove they remain retrievable. It reports the complete planned action count, sample failures, and whether new restore writes would be reversible. The drill refuses truncated scans and passes through the regional cost-and-permission preflight before making AWS requests.

sections.heading: Restore Semantics
sections.content: On a versioning-enabled bucket, restoring copies historical bytes into a new latest version and creates delete markers for keys that should be absent. Existing history is retained. Versioning-suspended buckets are clearly warned because the null version can be replaced in place. For large histories, narrow the prefix until the scan is complete.

sections.heading: Forecast and Anomaly Baseline
sections.content: Cost Autopilot uses actual account-wide Amazon S3 UnblendedCost returned by Cost Explorer. It projects the current UTC calendar month from month-to-date spend and compares that forecast with the median of up to five completed months. Variance of 20% enters Watch and 50% enters High anomaly. Spend without a historical baseline is labelled New spend instead of manufacturing an infinite percentage.
tips: Forecast confidence is low during the first three UTC days, medium through day nine, and high afterward.

Open Operate → Cost Explorer or search Cost Explorer in the command palette for account-wide spend, even without a bucket selected. The Daily/Monthly selector changes the account chart's aggregation; bucket tag breakdowns and Cost Autopilot remain monthly. The Period selector looks back 3, 6 (default) or 13 months, the most Cost Explorer allows. Cost Explorer data can lag and forecast accuracy depends on how evenly spend accumulates during the month.

Cost Explorer answers are cached per connection for 6 hours (spend) to 24 hours (access check and active tags) and are not retried automatically; if access fails, the panel says whether you are not signed in, access is denied, Cost Explorer is not enabled, or the error is unknown. A separate notice appears when no cost-allocation tags are active.

sections.heading: Local Guardrail
sections.content: The monthly USD guardrail is stored on this application installation. It compares the month-end forecast with a personal threshold but does not create, modify, or replace AWS Budgets. Use AWS Budgets and billing alerts for authoritative account notifications.

sections.heading: Prioritized Investigations
sections.content: The latest month's Cost Explorer usage types are ranked by share. Material storage, request, transfer, retrieval, restore, and early-deletion drivers produce targeted investigations for lifecycle and versions, Local Index and Inventory, cross-Region or CloudFront paths, and storage-class churn. The displayed amount is forecast cost at risk—not guaranteed savings.

sections.heading: Permissions and Scope
sections.content: Account forecasting requires ce:GetCostAndUsage. Per-bucket actual cost still requires an activated cost-allocation tag whose value identifies the bucket. Cost Autopilot performs no AWS mutation and does not automatically apply lifecycle or storage-class changes.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Copy, move or migrate data between buckets, including buckets in other saved AWS profiles and accounts. Open it from Browse › More › Transfer this prefix, from an object's Transfer action, from the selection bar, or from the command palette.

sections.heading: Start a Transfer
sections.content: Choose an operation (Copy, Move after verification, or Migrate bucket), the source and destination profile, bucket and prefix, and how existing objects are handled: skip (default), overwrite, keep both or copy only if newer. Options cover all versions, destination encryption and preserving metadata, tags and storage class. A preflight check of both identities and buckets is required before you can review the cost and start.
tips: The transfer path is chosen automatically — direct inside AWS when possible, otherwise a secure local relay — or you can pick S3 Batch Operations for very large jobs.
Move deletes a source object only after its copy is verified.

sections.heading: Transfer Center
sections.content: The Transfer Center tab lists jobs with progress, copied, skipped, deleted and failed counts. Jobs survive restarts; interrupted jobs wait for you to review them. Pause, resume, retry failures, cancel, or clear finished jobs. The last 250 finished jobs are kept.

sections.heading: Migrate a Bucket
sections.content: Migrate bucket copies a whole bucket to another profile, creating the destination if needed. It can also migrate safe bucket settings (versioning, encryption, lifecycle, CORS, tags, website, ownership, Public Access Block and Object Lock) and, if you choose, delete the source once it is verified empty.

sections.heading: Compare & Sync
sections.content: Compare & sync keeps a relationship between two locations. Choose Update only or Exact mirror and a Fast (size + ETag) or Verified (checksum) comparison. A reconciliation preview must pass the safety limits before the relationship can be saved. Optional schedules run while Buckets is open. Mirror deletions need explicit approval and are capped per run.
tips: Run history keeps the last 250 runs with counts and warnings.
Press Cmd+K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) and search for "Compare & sync relationships" or "Transfer Center" to open a tab directly.

commands.title: Transfer object to another bucket or profile
Transfer this prefix to another bucket or profile

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: A deep link opens Buckets at a specific bucket and folder, optionally with a profile label and region. Share one with a teammate to hand off a location. Create it from Browse › More › Deep Links, Operate › Speed, or the command palette.

sections.heading: Link Format
sections.content: Links look like serverlesscreed-buckets://bucket/<name>?prefix=…&profile=…&region=…. They never contain credentials and do not grant access — the recipient needs their own authorised profile. Buckets validates every part of an incoming link and ignores anything unexpected.
tips: Edit the prefix before copying to link to a different folder.

commands.title: Share a deep link to this location

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Storage Lens (top bar › … › Storage Lens) shows account-wide storage metrics from your Amazon S3 Storage Lens configurations.

sections.heading: Using Storage Lens
sections.content: Pick a configuration to see its storage size, object count and bucket count over the last 7, 14 or 30 days, with the latest value and a trend line. You can enable or disable a configuration from the same dialog. Create configuration adds a dashboard: a name, its scope (all buckets in the account, selected buckets, or selected Regions), optional activity metrics and advanced cost-optimization and data-protection metrics (the form notes that these are billed monthly per million objects monitored, while free metrics cost nothing), and an optional export bucket and prefix. Delete asks for confirmation; its metrics stop updating and exported files already in S3 are kept. The default dashboard can't be deleted — disable it instead.
tips: Metrics come from CloudWatch, so the dashboard must publish CloudWatch metrics.
Listing configurations needs s3:ListStorageLensConfigurations.
An export bucket's policy must allow storage-lens.s3.amazonaws.com to write; Buckets doesn't change it.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Mount an SFTP, FTPS or WebDAV server (including Nextcloud, ownCloud and SharePoint) as a local folder. Open it from Home › SFTP / WebDAV / FTPS or the command palette. This feature needs rclone installed on your computer.

sections.heading: Connecting
sections.content: Choose the protocol and enter the host (or WebDAV URL), port, username and password or SSH key file. Test connection lists the remote folder without mounting. WebDAV must use HTTPS except for local addresses.
steps: Choose the protocol.
Enter the connection details and Test connection.
Choose an empty local folder and Mount.

sections.heading: Mounts and Safety
sections.content: Mounts are read-only unless you allow writes and deletes. Passwords are never saved or logged. Active mounts are listed with Unmount; close open files if a mount does not stop cleanly.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The Operate overview includes a storage topology panel for S3 Express One Zone directory buckets and Multi-Region Access Points.

sections.heading: Directory Buckets
sections.content: Search for S3 Express, directory buckets, or TC-EXPRESS-001 in the top-bar search or Cmd/Ctrl+K, then choose Browse S3 Express directory buckets. The current region’s directory bucket list loads automatically. In Operate → Overview → AWS storage topology, load directory buckets in the current region, create one in an Availability Zone (names end in --zone-id--x-s3), test a session, or delete an empty bucket by typing its name. Click a bucket name or Browse objects to open its read-only browser. Open prefixes, use Load more for additional results, and select an object to read up to 64 KiB of its content. Text is displayed as UTF-8 and binary data as hex; partial previews and empty objects are labeled. Use Up one prefix or Bucket root to navigate back, and Refresh objects to reload the current prefix. The AWS SDK manages zonal session authentication for listing and reading.

sections.heading: Multi-Region Access Points
sections.content: Create an access point over two or more regional buckets (public access is always blocked), check the asynchronous creation status, and adjust failover routing: active-active, or fail over to one region after typing FAILOVER. AWS usually redirects new traffic within about two minutes.
tips: Deleting an access point or bucket requires typing its exact name.

commands.title: AWS storage topology & Multi-Region Access Points

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: The Money leaks report scans every bucket in the active AWS account (or one bucket) for patterns that quietly add to the S3 and CloudFront bill, estimates what each costs per month, and offers a reviewed one-click lifecycle fix where one exists. Open it from the command palette (Money leaks report) or from Find money leaks in Costs & Cost Autopilot.
steps: Press ⌘K / Ctrl+K and run Money leaks report, or Money leaks for this bucket with a bucket selected.
Choose the Standard-data age threshold, the suggested transition (Intelligent-Tiering or Standard-IA), the request budget and the maximum number of buckets.
Start the scan and approve the cost and permission review.
Review findings by finding or by bucket, open Details for the evidence, and use the fix button to review the exact lifecycle change.

sections.heading: What the Scan Finds
sections.content: Incomplete multipart uploads older than 7 days that no AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload rule covers (parts are billed but invisible in listings). Versioned buckets with noncurrent versions and no NoncurrentVersionExpiration rule. Expired object delete markers with no versions behind them. Standard-class data older than the chosen age with no transition rule. Buckets that receive S3 server access logs, CloudTrail logs or CloudFront standard logs but have no expiration for that prefix. Public or static-website buckets with high BytesDownloaded, only when CloudWatch request metrics are configured. CloudFront invalidation paths above the 1,000 free paths per month.
tips: Uploads that Buckets itself is writing right now are excluded from the multipart finding.
Rules filtered by object tags or size cannot be evaluated against unseen objects, so they are treated as covering the data to avoid false alarms.

sections.heading: Estimates vs Billed
sections.content: Every dollar amount is labelled. Estimate means measured bytes, objects or paths multiplied by bundled public on-demand list prices for the bucket's Region; it excludes taxes, credits, private pricing and Free Tier. At least means the evidence was sampled or capped, so the real amount is higher. Savings is what the fix removes; cost at risk is what the pattern costs today. Billed figures come from the existing Cost Explorer integration (account-wide S3 spend for the last complete month, split into storage, requests and data transfer) and are shown next to the estimates, never mixed into them. Because Cost Explorer charges $0.01 per request, they load only when you choose Load billed spend (two requests), unless figures for the same connection are already cached from Bucket settings.
tips: Billed figures need ce:GetCostAndUsage. Without it the report still works with estimates.
Standard data without S3 Inventory has no reliable age, so the report says insufficient data and shows only a ceiling. Build the Local index for an exact figure.

sections.heading: Bounded Scan and Permissions
sections.content: The scan is read-only and runs only after the cost and permission review. A hard request budget (default 2,000, maximum 20,000) caps every AWS call; per bucket it reads one page of multipart uploads, sizes at most 20 of the oldest, and reads at most 5 pages of version history. Progress is shown live and Cancel stops the scan and keeps partial results. Denied or failed calls are listed under Coverage and limitations instead of failing the whole report. S3-compatible endpoints are not supported because they do not expose CloudWatch, CloudFront or Cost Explorer.

sections.heading: Per-Bucket Drill-Down
sections.content: Switch to By bucket to rank buckets by estimated monthly impact, then select a bucket to see only its findings, its Region, which data sources were available (lifecycle, multipart listing, version sample, CloudWatch, S3 Inventory) and any calls that were denied. Money leaks for this bucket runs a fresh scan limited to the selected bucket.

sections.heading: One-Click Lifecycle Fixes
sections.content: A fix never replaces your lifecycle configuration. Buckets reads the current rules exactly as S3 returns them, appends one new rule (for example buckets-money-leaks-abort-incomplete-multipart), and shows the exact diff and the full resulting configuration. Existing rules keep their order, IDs, scope and actions, and the transition minimum object size is preserved. A rule that still uses the deprecated rule-level Prefix (written by the old lifecycle API) is rewritten as the equivalent Filter prefix so the configuration uses one rule format, as AWS recommends for new writes; it matches the same objects, and the rewrite appears in the diff with a warning. If an enabled rule with identical settings already exists nothing changes; if the rule ID is taken by a different rule, the new rule gets a numbered suffix. Applying requires your confirmation, the cost review, and a profile that is not in read-only mode. Just before writing, Buckets re-reads the configuration and refuses to apply if it changed since your review.
tips: Expiration, noncurrent-version expiration and multipart abort rules permanently remove data once S3 runs them, usually within a day or two.

A log expiration rule with no prefix expires every current object in the bucket. Use it only for buckets that hold nothing but logs; Buckets asks you to type the bucket name before it applies such a rule.
Read-only profiles show the diff but block the apply; temporarily unlock in Operate → Guardrails.

sections.heading: Export
sections.content: Export Markdown produces a shareable report with a summary, a findings table, per-finding evidence and the coverage notes. Export CSV produces one row per finding with amount, amount kind, estimate/billed label, data quality and the recommended fix; spreadsheet formulas are neutralized. When Cost Explorer data is loaded, the billed S3 spend is included and labelled billed.

sections.heading: What It Checks
sections.content: Virtual drive setup guide detects your operating system and architecture, whether rclone is on the PATH Buckets started with, its version and build tags, and whether a FUSE layer is installed: macFUSE or FUSE-T on macOS, WinFsp on Windows, and /dev/fuse plus fusermount3 on Linux. Open it from the command palette or from the Virtual drive dialog when something is missing. Re-check runs the detection again.

sections.heading: macOS
sections.content: Install rclone from the official precompiled binary, not Homebrew: rclone.org states that the Homebrew build does not support rclone mount. The guide gives the exact curl commands for Apple Silicon (arm64) or Intel (amd64); downloading with curl avoids the Gatekeeper prompt a browser download triggers. If a Homebrew rclone is found, the guide flags it and shows brew uninstall rclone first. Then install macFUSE from macfuse.github.io, or FUSE-T from fuse-t.org, which needs no kernel extension. With macFUSE's kernel backend on Apple Silicon, the first use requires enabling system extensions and Reduced Security in Recovery, then allowing the extension and restarting.
tips: The guide confirms mount support by looking for the cmount tag in rclone version output.

sections.heading: Windows
sections.content: Install rclone with winget install Rclone.Rclone (or the official zip from rclone.org) and WinFsp with winget install -e --id WinFsp.WinFsp (or the installer from winfsp.dev). Quit and reopen Buckets afterwards so it sees the updated PATH.

sections.heading: Linux
sections.content: Install rclone with the official script (sudo -v ; curl https://rclone.org/install.sh | sudo bash) or your distribution's package, and the fuse3 package (apt, dnf or pacman). On recent Ubuntu, a fusermount3 permission error can come from AppArmor; the rclone documentation describes the workaround.

sections.heading: What Buckets Never Does
sections.content: Buckets never downloads, runs or approves installers, kernel extensions or drivers. Copy buttons put the exact command on your clipboard and Open official page links go only to rclone.org, macfuse.github.io, fuse-t.org, winfsp.dev and the projects' GitHub pages. The only program the check runs is rclone version on an rclone you already installed, without the network check option.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Folder Sync connects one local folder to one S3 bucket prefix. Push uploads local changes; Pull downloads remote changes. Automatic remote detection can use an S3-event SQS queue with scheduled polling as a fallback. Conflicting edits are never silently overwritten: compare them, keep either side, keep both, or resolve a selected batch.

sections.heading: Create a Profile
sections.content: A profile defines the local folder, S3 destination, filters, safety policy, and automatic behavior.
steps: Open Folder Sync from the sidebar or from a bucket workspace.
Choose an existing local folder, bucket, required non-root S3 prefix, and region.
Add optional include patterns to limit scope and exclude patterns to remove files from scope.
Choose whether local changes should auto-sync, whether S3 should be pulled on a schedule, and whether every push requires approval.
Leave Mirror local deletions to S3 off for non-destructive upload behavior. Enable it only when the S3 prefix should exactly mirror local deletions.
Choose Push local, Pull S3, or Safe merge for first-run reconciliation. Safe merge pulls first, preserves conflicts, then previews remaining uploads.
Create the profile and approve the billable operation before transfer begins.
tips: The first-run preview shows counts, total upload size, and a bounded file sample.
Require preview for every push pauses each push with changes until it is approved in the profile card, including deletions from S3 when Mirror local deletions to S3 is enabled.
Files under 100 MB are uploaded as a single request. Larger files use Buckets' own resumable multipart upload. Up to 5 files upload at once per profile and at most 10 across all profiles.
If a profile requires a preview for every push, a plan with no changes runs without waiting for approval.
Empty nested folders are preserved with zero-byte S3 folder markers.

sections.heading: Auto-Sync
sections.content: Auto-sync watches the local folder and pushes new or modified files after a short debounce. Scheduled pull checks the prefix at the selected interval. An optional SQS queue consumes S3 ObjectCreated/ObjectRemoved events for near-real-time selective pulls. Push and pull never run concurrently for the same profile.
tips: A new profile's watcher starts only after its first preview has been approved.
Use Pause to disable both automatic directions and Enable to resume the saved policy.
If the watched folder is moved or deleted, auto-sync stops automatically and the profile is marked with an error.
Auto-sync runs silently in the background — you don't need to keep the Folder Sync modal open.
If native file watching is unavailable, the modal shows a persistent polling-mode warning.
Automatic work honors the configured local-time transfer window, including overnight windows. Manual Sync Now and Pull remain available outside it.

sections.heading: Sync Profiles
sections.content: Profiles preserve local and remote locations, filters, deletion policy, preview requirements, automatic push/pull settings, transfer window, event queue, metadata policy, and independent upload/download bandwidth limits.
steps: Use Sync Now for a local-to-S3 push or Pull for S3-to-local reconciliation. Enter comma-separated files or folders in Selective pull paths to limit a pull.
Use the Auto-sync switch for local change watching and edit the profile to configure scheduled pull.
Use History to inspect recent runs and their per-file results. Export the audit trail as CSV or JSON.
Use Open folder to work in the real local mirror in Finder, Explorer, or the Linux file manager.
tips: Profiles are tied to your AWS account — switching accounts will only show profiles for the current account.

When you are signed in to your Buckets account, On your other devices lists the account's profiles from your other computers (device, local path, destination and last status). They are read-only here: a profile syncs only on the device that owns its folder.
Editing preserves all advanced settings and machine ownership metadata.
Enabled profiles cannot use the same or nested local roots, real-path aliases, or overlapping S3 prefixes.
When you log out, all active watchers and syncs are stopped automatically.

sections.heading: Safety Features
sections.content: Folder Sync includes several safety mechanisms to protect your data from accidental loss.
tips: Mass-delete protection: when S3 mirror deletion is enabled, a plan that removes at least 10 cached objects and 50% of the cache is paused for explicit approval.

When a file is deleted from S3 controls S3-to-local pulls: preserve local files, review before deleting each local copy, or delete local copies after guarded approval. It does not control deletions from S3 caused by removing local files. Uncached local files are never deleted.
Remote deletion is opt-in. With mirror deletion off, deleting a local file never deletes its S3 copy.
A suspicious deletion plan is paused and lists representative keys. It runs only after Approve and run is selected.

Multi-device conflicts show directly on the profile. Compare displays a bounded local/S3 text preview; Keep local authorizes one overwrite; Keep S3 downloads atomically; Keep both preserves a timestamped local copy.
Versions lists historical S3 versions. Restore local is non-mutating to S3; Rollback S3 + local copies the selected version back to the current key after billable approval.
File-level retry: Transient network errors are retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff. Permanent errors (like expired credentials) abort the sync immediately.
Credential expiry detection: If your AWS credentials expire mid-sync, the sync stops immediately instead of failing file by file.
Duplicate sync prevention: Only one sync can run per profile at a time.
Concurrent upload coordination: Regular file uploads and folder sync won't interfere with each other.
Unsafe S3 keys, Windows-invalid names, and local filename collisions are reported as pull failures rather than overwritten.
Symlinks are skipped by default. Follow internal allows only targets that remain inside the selected root. External links and loops remain blocked.
When metadata preservation is enabled, Folder Sync stores local modification time and POSIX mode in S3 metadata and reapplies them on pull where the OS supports it.

sections.heading: Exclude Patterns
sections.content: Use include patterns to create a positive allow-list and exclude patterns to remove matches from that list. Excludes always win. Enter one glob per line. Common examples: src/**, *.log, build/**, and .env. Temporary files, .git/**, .DS_Store, node_modules/**, Thumbs.db, and desktop.ini are excluded by default.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Buckets supports both dark and light themes. The theme can be toggled instantly, and your preference is saved across sessions so the app always launches with your chosen appearance.

sections.heading: Changing Theme
sections.content: Switching between dark and light mode is available from the top bar's … menu or the command palette.
steps: Open the … (More) menu at the right of the top bar and point to Theme.
Choose Light, Dark or System. The app switches instantly.
Your preference is saved and persisted across sessions.

sections.heading: System Detection
sections.content: The app detects your operating system's theme preference on first launch and sets the theme accordingly. If you prefer a different theme, you can override it at any time using the toggle.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Buckets is fully usable from the keyboard. The command palette is the fastest way to reach any feature.

sections.heading: Available Shortcuts
sections.content: These shortcuts work throughout the app.
tips: Cmd+K / Ctrl+K — open the command palette (works even while typing)
Shift+Enter in the palette — open the documentation for the highlighted command
Cmd+\ / Ctrl+\ — toggle the Inspector in Browse
Cmd+Shift+\ / Ctrl+Shift+\ — cycle the Inspector's permissions tab
Cmd+Enter / Ctrl+Enter — run the command in the AWS CLI console
Escape — close dialogs, menus and search
Enter or Space — open the focused folder or object
Arrow keys — move through results, menus and resize handles

sections.heading: Navigation
sections.content: Use Tab to move between controls, Enter to activate, and Escape to close any dialog or dropdown. Resize handles (sidebar, Inspector split) respond to the arrow keys, Home and End.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Get help or provide feedback directly from within Buckets. The support system makes it easy to report issues, suggest features, or ask questions.

sections.heading: Contacting Support
sections.content: Reach out to the Buckets team without leaving the app.
steps: Click the Support button in the sidebar footer.
Fill in your message describing the issue or feedback.
Optionally attach files for context.
Click Send.
tips: Include screenshots when reporting visual issues.
Mention your operating system and app version for faster resolution; the version is shown at the bottom of the profile menu.

sections.heading: Diagnostics
sections.content: When something goes wrong, attach a diagnostics report to your email. Contact support › Preview diagnostics shows the redacted report in a read-only box; Copy diagnostics then puts exactly that text on the clipboard and Save diagnostics… writes it to a text file. The command palette has "Copy diagnostics for support" too. The report holds the app, OS, Electron and Node versions, uptime, the sign-in method kind (SSO, CLI, static keys or S3-compatible — never account identifiers), the number of saved profiles, the last 50 captured errors (main process and renderer) and the last 200 lines of the local log.
tips: Keys, tokens, emails, account IDs, ARNs and file paths are removed. Bucket and object names in log lines may remain, as may an account ID written without an account label — review the text before sending. Nothing is sent automatically — you decide what to attach.
If Buckets hits an unexpected error, a dialog offers Copy diagnostics, Continue and Quit. It appears once per session so a crash loop cannot spam you.

sections.heading: Other Resources
sections.content: Visit the Buckets website for additional documentation and guides. Check for updates to ensure you're running the latest version with the newest features and bug fixes.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Choose the interface language from top bar › … › Language, or run "Language: <name>" from the command palette. English, Hindi, Spanish and Japanese are available for the main navigation and command centre; text that is not yet translated appears in English.

sections.heading: Saving
sections.content: The choice is saved on this device and applied immediately.

pages.title: Essentials Mode & What You Use S3 For

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Essentials mode keeps Buckets focused on the file browser: browse buckets and folders, upload, download, preview, rename, delete, tag and share. Workspaces, toolbar entries and sidebar items for the use cases you did not choose are hidden. Nothing is removed — every feature stays in the command palette (Cmd+K / Ctrl+K), deep links and keyboard shortcuts keep working, and you can switch to the full interface at any time.
tips: While Essentials is on, the top bar's … menu starts with "Showing Essentials" and "Show everything". Choose "Showing Essentials" to change your use cases.
Home shows how many capabilities are hidden and still finds every capability when you search.

sections.heading: Choosing Your Use Cases
sections.content: On a new installation, Buckets asks "What do you use S3 for?" once, right after your first successful connection. Pick any combination; the file browser is always included. You can reopen the picker from top bar › … › Showing Essentials (or › What I use S3 for when everything is shown), or by running "Choose what you use S3 for" in the command palette.
steps: Connect a profile. The picker opens when your buckets load.
Select one or more use cases.
Choose Continue to use Essentials for them, or Show everything for the full interface.
Choose Skip for now (or press Esc) to start with Files & sharing.

sections.heading: What Each Use Case Shows
sections.content: Files & sharing: share links (Deep Links), Drop Zones, transfers between buckets and profiles, Folder Sync, SFTP/WebDAV mounts and the virtual drive. Websites & CDN: the CloudFront workspace, Build › Publish and website URLs. Data & analytics: Athena, Glue, S3 Tables, the inventory index, Storage Lens and S3 Select. AI & vectors: Build › AI retrieval with S3 Vectors and Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Automation: Build › Pipelines, Lambda triggers, developer tools, code generation, infrastructure export and the AWS CLI. Security & admin: the Operate workspace, security scanner, policies and Access Control, audit evidence, Time Travel, bucket settings and advanced bucket features.

sections.heading: Showing Everything
sections.content: Choose Show everything in the top bar's … menu, in the picker, or run "Show everything" from the command palette to see every workspace and tool. Run "Switch to Essentials mode" to go back; your previous use cases are kept.

sections.heading: Hidden Features Stay Reachable
sections.content: Type in the command palette to find any command, including hidden ones (marked "Hidden in Essentials"). Running one opens it as usual and offers "Always show <area>", which adds that area to your Essentials selection. A workspace you open this way stays in the sidebar while it is active.

sections.heading: Upgrading from an Earlier Version
sections.content: If this device already has Buckets settings, saved profiles or stored credentials, nothing is hidden after an update and the picker is not shown. You can opt in to Essentials mode at any time from the command palette or top bar › … › What I use S3 for. The preference is stored on this device and kept when you log out.

commands.title: Choose what you use S3 for

sections.heading: What the Workbench Does
sections.content: The former Powerhouse feature set is now divided between two focused workspaces without changing its AWS handlers. Build contains Lakehouse, Publish, AI retrieval, and Pipelines. Operate contains Guardrails and Speed and links to the existing CloudFront and Folder Sync surfaces. Both workspaces share the active profile, region, selected bucket, jobs, and notifications.

sections.heading: Opening a Feature
sections.content: Select Build at the top of the sidebar for Lakehouse, Publish, AI Retrieval, and Event Pipelines. Select Operate for Guardrails, Audit, and Speed. You can also press Command-K on macOS or Control-K on Windows and Linux and search for any of these tools directly.
steps: Sign in to the AWS profile and region that own the resources you want to manage.
Select Build or Operate from the workspace switcher at the top of the sidebar.
Choose a workbench tab. Build and Operate share the active profile, region, and selected bucket.
Select an S3 bucket before opening bucket-scoped Pipeline, Scan, or Deep Link tools.
tips: A profile or region switch changes the AWS resources returned by the workbench.
Build and Operate actions also appear in the command palette, even while another workspace is open.

sections.heading: AWS Permissions
sections.content: Buckets uses the active profile's credentials and does not create a separate cloud identity. Grant only the actions needed for the tabs you use. Common action families are s3tables, athena, glue, cloudfront, s3vectors, bedrock, lambda, s3, sns, and sqs. Site deployment also needs permission to create or configure an S3 bucket, Origin Access Control, distribution, bucket policy, and invalidation. Read-only mode can further restrict mutations locally, but it does not replace IAM.
tips: AccessDenied usually means the active identity lacks the displayed service action or is constrained by an SCP, permission boundary, or resource policy.
Use separate least-privilege AWS profiles for staging and production.
Private keys and AWS secrets should never be pasted into documentation, object metadata, audit details, or Lambda test events.

sections.heading: Mutation Safety
sections.content: Mutating Powerhouse flows require an explicit confirmation and are evaluated again in the Electron main process. When the active profile is read-only and its temporary unlock has expired, the request returns READ_ONLY_PROFILE without calling AWS. All application mutation handlers—including existing bucket and object tools—write success, failure, or blocked results to the local audit log.

sections.heading: Browse S3 Tables
sections.content: The Lakehouse tab follows the S3 Tables hierarchy: table bucket, namespace, then Iceberg table. Selecting a table loads its ARN, maintenance configuration, and last maintenance job status. Results are region-specific and paginated by the AWS service.
steps: Open Build and select Lakehouse.
Choose a table bucket in the first column.
Choose a namespace in the second column.
Choose an Iceberg table in the third column.
Review compaction, snapshot-management settings, and the most recent job status in Iceberg Maintenance.
tips: An empty first column can mean the region has no table buckets or the profile lacks s3tables:ListTableBuckets.
Maintenance status is independent for compaction and snapshot management.

sections.heading: Make an S3 Prefix Queryable
sections.content: Use the Athena Workbench's Create table from S3 prefix flow for CSV, TSV, JSON, Parquet, or ORC data. The schema inference engine samples small CSV or JSON objects, handles quoted delimiters and JSON Lines, widens integer-plus-decimal fields to double, and marks missing values nullable. Review inferred names and types before creating a Glue table. Parquet and ORC retain their native columnar schema through their SerDe configuration.
steps: Select a bucket and prefix containing one consistent file format.
Open Athena Workbench and choose Create table from S3 prefix.
Select or create a Glue database and enter a valid table name.
Review columns, partitions, delimiter, and header-row settings.
Create the table, then run the generated SELECT query in Athena.
tips: Keep mixed schemas in separate prefixes; sampling cannot make incompatible records safe.
Glue and Athena identifiers must start with a letter or underscore and contain only letters, numbers, and underscores.
The S3 location should end with a slash so Athena scans the prefix rather than a similarly named key.

sections.heading: Iceberg Time Travel
sections.content: Time Travel generates Athena Iceberg syntax for a timestamp or snapshot version without changing the table. Timestamp values are converted to an explicit UTC timestamp. Snapshot IDs must be non-negative integers. Start with LIMIT 100, verify the result, and then adapt the query in Athena Workbench.
steps: Select an Iceberg table.
Enter the Athena database and an ISO timestamp, or provide a snapshot ID.
Generate the query-as-of SQL.
Review and run the SQL in Athena Workbench.

sections.heading: Query Cost, Partition Health & Catalog Hygiene
sections.content: Athena reports bytes scanned for every completed query. Buckets estimates run cost from that value and raises partition advice when a large scan filters on likely partition columns such as year, month, day, date, region, tenant_id, or account_id. Schema-drift checks compare sampled columns with the Glue catalog and separate added, missing, and type-changed fields. Treat estimates as planning guidance; AWS billing, compression, result reuse, and regional pricing can change the final charge.
