pages.title: Publish Pipeline: Folder to Live Site

sections.heading: Deployment Architecture
sections.content: The Publish flow deploys a local folder to a private S3 bucket and serves it through an Origin Access Control (OAC) backed CloudFront distribution. Public bucket access stays blocked. CloudFront redirects viewers to HTTPS, enables compression, uses HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and applies the AWS managed CachingOptimized policy. The distribution uses the default *.cloudfront.net certificate; the TLSv1.2_2021 minimum protocol it requests takes effect only once a custom ACM certificate is attached, because CloudFront ignores it for the default certificate. HTML receives must-revalidate caching; fingerprinted assets receive a long immutable cache lifetime.

sections.heading: Preview and Deploy
sections.content: Deployments are incremental. Buckets hashes local files, compares them with remote ETags, and classifies keys as upload, unchanged, or remove. Symlinks are skipped. The preview is read-only; AWS changes begin only after Confirm deploy.
steps: Open Publish and choose the local website folder.
Enter a globally unique lowercase bucket name and an environment such as staging or production.
Click Preview diff and review upload, unchanged, and remove counts.
Confirm the deploy. If the bucket does not exist, Buckets creates it with encryption and Block Public Access.
Wait for uploads, CloudFront creation or reuse, bucket policy configuration, and cache invalidation to finish.

Save staging and production as separate deployment environments when they use the same local folder. Each environment remembers its bucket, region, distribution, and saved-account ID. Selecting it switches through the existing multi-account credential workflow before loading its values; missing or expired accounts fail closed. A successful deploy updates only that environment's distribution association, so staging and production never reuse each other's CDN accidentally.
Open the returned HTTPS CloudFront domain after the distribution reaches Deployed state.
tips: The remove count is applied only when delete-extraneous is enabled in the deploy plan.
Bucket names cannot look like IP addresses, contain adjacent dots, or use AWS-reserved prefixes and suffixes.
A failed deployment may leave successfully created AWS resources. Review the audit entry and AWS resource state before retrying.

sections.heading: Incremental Invalidations
sections.content: After a deploy, changed and removed keys become targeted CloudFront invalidation paths. The successful deploy also associates that bucket and region with its distribution. Later Folder Sync completions automatically invalidate the exact keys that S3 accepted, including both paths of a rename. Duplicates and leading slashes are normalized. CloudFront accepts at most 3,000 paths per invalidation; when a change set exceeds that limit, Buckets safely falls back to /*. An invalidation permission or quota failure is reported separately and never mislabels a completed S3 sync as failed.

sections.heading: Cache Behavior Visualizer
sections.content: Choose a live distribution and enter a request path to see which ordered behavior, origin, and cache policy handle it. CloudFront evaluates ordered behaviors from top to bottom and uses the first match, then falls back to the default behavior. The miss debugger reads recent standard logs from the distribution's configured S3 logging bucket, supports gzip files, skips malformed or oversized files, and uses result type, query string, cookies, and authorization evidence from a selected request. Standard logging must already be enabled in CloudFront, and the active profile needs read access to its log bucket.

sections.heading: Signed Delivery and Edge Functions
sections.content: The delivery inventory shows CloudFront key groups and CloudFront Functions associated with the active account. The signed-delivery manager can select the first public key from a key group or accept a public-key ID directly, then create a SHA-256 signed URL or signed cookies with 5-minute, 1-hour, 1-day, or 7-day expiry presets and an optional IPv4 CIDR restriction. Wildcard resources are supported for cookies, not individual signed URLs. The PEM private key is read locally by the main process, limited to 64 KB, validated before use, and never persisted or included in audit details. Select a CloudFront Function to load its DEVELOPMENT source and ETag. Save validates the handler and 10 KB UTF-8 limit, and uses If-Match so a concurrent AWS edit cannot be overwritten silently. Tests run against the saved ETag and publish stays disabled until that exact ETag passes; any edit or save clears the test gate. CloudFront Functions appear directly in Build → Publish under Signed delivery & edge code. Refresh delivery tools after creating an approved test function in AWS Console. Failed sample events keep publish disabled; publishing retests the same saved ETag before updating LIVE. Refresh associations to inspect behavior, event type, and distribution deployment status. Publishing does not create an association; configure any approved LIVE association in AWS Console. Lambda@Edge uses a separate AWS Console workflow in us-east-1. The S3 Lambda Builder does not provide Lambda@Edge event testing or association.

sections.heading: Vector Buckets and Indexes
sections.content: The AI Retrieval tab exhausts regional S3 vector-bucket and index pages with repeated-cursor guards. Index details include dimensions, distance metric, data type, non-filterable metadata keys, and a sample of vector keys. Counting reads key-only pages and stops at 100,000 by default; a ≥ marker identifies capped counts instead of presenting them as exact. Small indexes are counted with a single request; larger ones are counted with eight parallel ListVectors segments, each with its own repeated-cursor guard, under a fixed request budget, and the first failing segment stops the rest. Click any sample key to open it in the vector inspector. Select an index whose dimensions match the embedding model you intend to use.
steps: Open AI retrieval and select a vector bucket.
Select an index and verify its dimensions and distance metric.
Enter natural-language query text in Similarity Playground.
Run the query and inspect result keys, distances, and metadata.
Use source bucket and key metadata to open the original object preview.

sections.heading: Similarity Playground
sections.content: Choose Text or Vector input. Text is embedded through Amazon Bedrock Titan Text Embeddings V2 (256, 512, or 1,024 dimensions). Vector input accepts a JSON array or comma-separated numbers for an index of any dimension, so indexes built with other embedding models can be searched without Bedrock. Malformed vectors, filters, and topK outside 1–100 are rejected locally; Buckets then reads the index's real dimension and non-filterable keys before querying, so wrong-length vectors, out-of-float32 values, and text over 50,000 characters never reach QueryVectors. An optional metadata filter supports implicit equality plus $eq, $ne, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $in, $nin, $exists, $and, and $or; unknown operators, wrong operand types, and keys the index marked non-filterable fail locally with a precise message, and text queries validate the filter before paying for an embedding. Results show distance and metadata, an Inspect action, and an object preview when metadata uses s3Uri/s3_uri or source-bucket/source-key conventions.
steps: Select a vector index.
Choose Text (Titan V2) or Vector input and enter the query.
Optionally add a metadata filter such as {"category": "manual", "year": {"$gte": 2024}}.
Set Top K, run the query, and review the cost preflight.
Inspect a result or preview its source object.
tips: Smaller distance usually means greater similarity, but interpretation depends on the index metric.
Metadata filters should be tested on a small topK before broad retrieval.
Use Find similar in the vector inspector to query with an existing vector.
Bedrock model access must be enabled in the selected region.

sections.heading: Vector Inspector and JSONL Transfer
sections.content: The vector inspector fetches up to 100 keys with GetVectors and shows each vector's length, leading values, and metadata, and lists keys that were not found. Find similar copies a vector into the Similarity Playground; Copy vector puts its values on the clipboard. Export writes the whole index (up to 1,000,000 vectors) as JSON Lines—one {key, vector, metadata} object per line—to a temporary file that is renamed only after the last page succeeds; an export that fails with an error removes the temporary file. Import accepts .jsonl or .ndjson files up to 1 GiB and 1,000,000 vectors in the same format (data.float32 is also accepted). The file is chosen in a system dialog and validated end to end against the index's live dimension—invalid JSON, missing or duplicate keys, wrong lengths, non-finite values, non-object metadata, and metadata over 40 KB are reported with their line number—before anything is written. After the cost preflight, vectors are written in batches of up to 500 (smaller for large vectors); the import is blocked for read-only profiles, is tied to the AWS profile and index that reviewed it, refuses a file whose content changed after review, and on failure reports how many vectors were already written. AWS can still reject a batch for limits checked only by the service, such as filterable metadata size. Completed and failed exports and imports are recorded in the local audit log.
steps: Select a vector index.
Enter vector keys (one per line) or click a key or Inspect result, then choose Get vectors.
Use Export index… to save the index as JSONL.
Use Choose JSONL file… to validate a file, review the count and sample keys, then import.
tips: Existing vectors with the same keys are overwritten by an import.
Exported files are a portable backup and can be imported into another index with the same dimension.

sections.heading: Prefix to Knowledge Base
sections.content: The Knowledge Base flow connects an S3 prefix to an S3 Vectors-backed Bedrock Knowledge Base. It requires validated IAM role, embedding-model, and vector-index ARNs, plus a source bucket and normalized optional prefix. Fixed-size chunking must be 20–8,192 tokens with 0–99 percent overlap; invalid values are rejected rather than silently clamped. After explicit review, Buckets creates the Knowledge Base, creates its retained S3 data source, and starts the initial sync. A later-stage failure reports any Knowledge Base or data-source IDs already created.
steps: Choose the source bucket and document prefix.
Select the target S3 vector index and compatible embedding model.
Provide a Bedrock Knowledge Base service role with source and vector-store permissions.
Configure chunk size and overlap, then review the resource plan.
Create the Knowledge Base and data source.
Start ingestion and monitor document statistics or failure reasons.
tips: Keep PDFs and documents stable during ingestion to avoid inconsistent snapshots.
The data deletion policy retains source-derived vector data when a self-managed data source is removed; review AWS resources before cleanup.

sections.heading: Ingestion Monitor and Cost Lens
sections.content: Knowledge Base, data-source, job, and document pages are exhausted with repeated-cursor and page-limit guards. Select a job to refresh its exact statistics and top-level failure reasons. The document list separates failed, partially indexed, metadata-failed, not-found, and ignored documents with identifiers and status reasons. Re-sync starts a billable ingestion job only after confirmation and refreshes the monitor. The cost lens uses the selected index's counted vectors and real dimensions, with adjustable monthly embedding tokens and queries. It separates storage, embedding, and query estimates and labels a capped vector count as a lower bound. Rates are explicit planning assumptions, not a replacement for Cost Explorer or the current AWS pricing page.

commands.title: Create a Knowledge Base from a prefix

sections.heading: Pipeline Graph
sections.content: The Pipelines tab reads the selected bucket's notification configuration and draws one topology covering Lambda, SNS, SQS, and the default EventBridge bus. Each route shows all configured S3 events plus prefix/suffix filters, or explicitly says it applies to all matching keys. Duplicate destinations share one typed node while retaining separate event routes, and destination totals make missing integrations visible.
steps: Select an S3 bucket in the Storage view.
Open Build, then Pipelines.
Review every destination and event filter.
Use Trigger Management for configuration changes.

sections.heading: Test-Fire an S3 Event
sections.content: Test-fire creates the native S3 notification shape with one ObjectCreated:Put record, URL-encodes the chosen key, and invokes a Lambda destination from the displayed pipeline synchronously. A review names the exact region, function, bucket, and key before confirmation. Status, function error, response payload, and decoded Lambda tail logs appear separately inline. This invokes the real function and can cause downstream effects, so it respects profile read-only mode.
steps: Choose a representative object key; it does not have to be uploaded by the test-fire action.
Enter the Lambda function name or ARN.
Review the target account, region, bucket, key, and function.
Confirm the invocation and inspect status, payload, function error, and logs.
tips: Use a dedicated test function or staging profile when the handler writes data or sends messages.
The synthesized event uses a placeholder requester, request ID, ETag, and source IP.

sections.heading: Pipeline Templates
sections.content: Three S3-focused starting points are included: thumbnail/resize, virus-scan quarantine, and CSV-to-S3-Table ingestion. Selecting one generates a native S3 Records handler scaffold, exact prefix/suffix notification filters, least-purpose IAM action list, and a copyable SAM template for the selected bucket. Open Configured Lambda Builder carries runtime, function name, event, filters, description, and SAM format into the existing review/deploy flow. Application-specific image libraries, malware engines, and Iceberg append logic remain explicit implementation points rather than hidden dependencies.

sections.heading: Per-Profile Read-Only Mode
sections.content: Read-only mode is stored locally per AWS profile and enforced in the main process for both Powerhouse and existing application mutations. Profile names containing a distinct prod or production tag default to a hard read-only state and cannot disable it; they can only use a time-boxed unlock. The guard blocks creates, uploads, overwrites, deletes, copies, moves, restores, lifecycle edits, deploys, publishes, invalidations, and similar changes. Read operations remain available. A temporary unlock requires the exact word UNLOCK and expires after 1–60 minutes.
steps: Switch to the production AWS profile you want to protect.
Open Guardrails and enable read-only mode.
Verify that the profile card says Mutations blocked.
When an approved change is needed, create a short temporary unlock and perform only the reviewed operation.
Confirm the operation appears in the audit log, then allow the unlock to expire.
tips: Read-only mode is a local safety layer. IAM and AWS Organizations policies remain the authoritative cloud controls.
Profiles without stable names use the active-profile fallback, so name production profiles explicitly.

sections.heading: Dry-Run Diffs and Undo
sections.content: Destructive bulk workflows are reviewed before execution. Bulk delete lists every selected file and folder root and explicitly marks recursive descendants. Bulk tagging shows the exact object-key list plus set/merge/clear additions and removals. Lifecycle add, edit, and delete stage a JSON before/after diff and do not call AWS until confirmation. Successful app-initiated object delete, upload, copy, move, rename, and overwrite calls create a 30-minute local undo entry. On a versioned bucket, undo removes the matching latest delete marker or copies the immediately previous version into a new latest version. Expired entries, unversioned keys, missing prior versions, or a latest version older than the recorded mutation fail closed. Folder-recursive deletes are excluded because they cannot be represented as one safely verifiable version action.

sections.heading: Local Audit Log
sections.content: The audit ledger keeps the 10,000 newest mutation records with timestamp, active profile, semantic or legacy IPC operation, resource, success/failed/blocked outcome, and safe error detail. The main-process wrapper covers legacy mutations while Powerhouse records its semantic operations without duplicate wrapper rows. Case-insensitive search spans who, when, what, outcome, and detail; outcome and result-limit filters are validated. Export JSON or CSV for review or incident response. Files are written with owner-only permissions where the operating system supports them.
tips: The audit log is local to this app installation; it is not AWS CloudTrail and can be cleared with application data.
Use CloudTrail when you need authoritative identity, source IP, and account-wide API history.
Do not store secrets or sensitive object contents in mutation descriptions.

sections.heading: Scheduled Security Scans
sections.content: Schedule security scans at a whole-hour cadence from 1 hour to 30 days. Each schedule is bound to the signed-in profile and verified AWS account/principal in the selected Region. It persists locally and is checked every minute and at startup. Overdue scans wait for the matching authenticated profile; busy scans and failures before starting do not consume a cadence. Pause works without AWS authentication, and resuming the same cadence preserves an overdue run. Interrupted scan history is reconciled without opening the scanner UI and retries on the next tick. Invalid saved timing or an unbound legacy schedule requires explicit reconfiguration. Scheduled scans enable per-object ACL checks and require complete coverage within the default 5,000-object limit; denied reads or capped listings fail visibly and cannot replace the last successful public-access baseline. Content sampling limits still apply. A successful run compares public-access fingerprints with the previous successful run for this schedule; the first run establishes a zero-delta baseline. Guardrails shows the outcome, run ID/error, newly public/resolved counts and up to 25 new keys. Scheduling runs only while Buckets is open; it does not run as an operating-system or cloud task.
steps: Select the target bucket and open Guardrails.
Schedule a daily scan or choose another supported cadence.
Keep Buckets running at the due time.
Open Security Scanner to compare the newest run with earlier findings and remediate newly public or sensitive objects.

commands.title: Search and export the audit log

sections.heading: Large-Bucket Performance
sections.content: For buckets with a successful Inventory snapshot, the normal hierarchical object browser uses the local SQLite index by default—not only the separate search modal. It supports folders and opaque local pagination, shows the measured query time and snapshot age, and never mixes local tokens with S3 continuation tokens. Buckets without a completed index use live S3. The product targets under 250 ms for an indexed first page and under 150 ms to open the preview shell; the on-screen timing makes regressions observable rather than assumed. Actual object content still depends on S3 latency, object size, storage class, network conditions, and credentials.
tips: Configure and ingest S3 Inventory for very large buckets.
A stale index can be fast but incomplete; refresh it before compliance or deletion decisions.
Use a narrow prefix and pagination when a bucket is not indexed.

sections.heading: Buckets Deep Links
sections.content: A deep link has the form serverlesscreed-buckets://bucket/BUCKET?prefix=PREFIX&profile=PROFILE&region=REGION. The legacy s3console:// scheme remains accepted for existing links. Bucket and prefix values are URL-encoded. Opening a valid link focuses Buckets, resolves the exact named Saved Account when a profile differs, switches credentials, sets the target region, selects the bucket, and navigates to the prefix. If the profile is unavailable or switching fails, navigation stops before selecting the resource. Malformed protocols, credentials, ports, fragments, bucket names, prefixes, profiles, and regions are rejected with visible feedback. Cold-start URLs are retained until the renderer is ready; later links supersede older switches still in flight.
steps: In Browse, select the bucket and prefix, then open More → Deep Links. You can also use Operate → Open speed tools → Shareable deep links.
Verify the prefilled prefix, profile, and region. Edit the prefix if needed; leave it empty for the bucket root.
Copy the generated link and share it only with teammates who already have appropriate AWS access.
Open the link and verify the active profile and account before changing data.
tips: Deep links contain resource names and profile labels but never AWS credentials.
If the named profile is unavailable, the link fails closed; save or activate that account, then open the link again.

sections.heading: Transfer Engine
sections.content: Local file uploads and Folder Sync durably persist multipart upload IDs and verified source identities so interrupted large transfers can resume; small files use checksum-protected single PUTs. URL uploads first use validator-protected HTTP Range requests to build a private local recovery spool, then continue through the same resumable multipart queue; the spool is removed after success or explicit cancellation. Glacier restore is an asynchronous AWS job rather than a local byte transfer, so it is tracked in the restore queue and does not use multipart or local bandwidth. Server-side S3 copies likewise do not consume local bandwidth. The global Unlimited, 1, 5, 20 MiB/s, and validated custom presets apply per stream to newly started local-file, URL, and Folder Sync uploads; a stricter per-profile Folder Sync limit still wins. The consolidated panel shows active and resumable uploads, active/pending sync files, and the latest restore requests. Existing upload and sync progress surfaces retain pause, cancellation, and per-file detail.
tips: Use a conservative bandwidth preset when transfers compete with video calls or production traffic.
Canceling a multipart transfer should abort its AWS multipart upload; use Multipart Management to find abandoned parts after crashes.
Closing the app while transfers are active prompts before shutdown.

sections.heading: Command Palette
sections.content: Press Command-K or Control-K from anywhere in the app. The palette contains one named destination for each of the 25 P1–P5 features. Commands use task-oriented aliases, so searches such as schema drift, signed cookies, document failures, test-fire, lifecycle diff, or undo land on the corresponding workflow. Build commands open Lakehouse, Publish, AI retrieval, or Pipelines; operational commands open Guardrails. Bucket-scoped flows still require a selected bucket and preserve their normal confirmation gates.

sections.heading: Empty or Missing Resources
sections.content: First verify the active profile and region. S3 Tables, S3 Vectors, Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Lambda functions, and S3 notification configurations are regional. CloudFront resources are global but still use the active credentials. Then check the relevant List or Get permission and any organization-level restrictions.

sections.heading: Common Validation Errors
sections.content: CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED means the operation was submitted without its reviewed confirmation. READ_ONLY_PROFILE means the local profile guard blocked a mutation. Invalid identifier errors protect generated Athena and Glue SQL. Vector dimension errors mean the Bedrock embedding size does not match the S3 vector index. Invalid bucket-name errors prevent names AWS will reject, including IP format and reserved suffixes.

sections.heading: Partial Resource Creation
sections.content: AWS workflows can span multiple services and are not always transactional. A site deployment can create a bucket or OAC before CloudFront fails; a Knowledge Base can be created before its data source fails. Read the failed audit entry, inspect the AWS resources that now exist, and either complete the workflow with the same settings or remove the partial resources after confirming they are unused.

sections.heading: Safe Recovery Checklist
sections.content: Do not repeatedly retry a failed mutation without inspecting state; retries can create duplicate global resources or incur charges.
steps: Open Guardrails and find the failed audit entry.
Record the profile, region, operation, resource, and AWS error code.
Refresh the relevant workbench browser to discover resources created before the failure.
Correct IAM, naming, quota, model-access, or configuration issues.
Preview the operation again and confirm only after the resulting diff is understood.

sections.heading: A Shared AWS Context
sections.content: Buckets organizes its capabilities into Home, Browse, Operate, and Build. These are workspace modes over the same signed-in AWS context, not separate products. Your active profile, region, selected bucket, transfers, synchronization jobs, and notifications remain available when you change workspaces.

sections.heading: Home
sections.content: Home is the Command Center. It provides quick actions, the current profile, region and bucket context, and a searchable directory of every capability. Selecting a capability opens its canonical workspace instead of duplicating the feature inside Home.
tips: Use Home when you know the outcome you want but not where the tool lives.
Capability badges identify actions that may create AWS cost or affect production resources.

sections.heading: Browse
sections.content: Browse is the familiar S3 resource workspace for buckets, prefixes, objects, previews, uploads, downloads, metadata, tags, search, and sharing. It remains the default during the workspace rollout so existing navigation and deep links keep their previous behavior.

sections.heading: Operate
sections.content: Operate groups security, recovery, audit, synchronization, transfer optimization, cost, and CloudFront delivery. Guardrails and Speed reuse the same tested AWS handlers that previously lived in the Powerhouse Workbench. Folder Sync and CloudFront continue to open their existing canonical surfaces.

sections.heading: Build
sections.content: Build contains Lakehouse, Publish, AI retrieval, and Pipeline workbenches. Use it for Athena, Glue, S3 Tables, Iceberg maintenance, S3 Vectors, Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Lambda event flows, and static deployment.

sections.heading: Moving Between Workspaces
sections.content: Use the four workspace buttons at the top of the sidebar. Command Palette actions route Guardrails and Speed to Operate and route Lakehouse, Publish, AI retrieval, and Pipelines to Build. Selecting a table bucket in Browse opens the matching S3 Tables context in Build.
steps: Select a bucket in Browse.
Open Operate to inspect or protect that bucket, or Build to create a workflow from it.
Return to Browse; the same bucket remains selected.
Open Home at any time to search the complete capability directory.

sections.heading: Reaching Any Feature
sections.content: Each workspace, workbench tab and panel is also a command palette entry (Cmd+K / Ctrl+K), so you can jump straight to, for example, Operate › Guardrails › Undo window.

sections.heading: Durable Transfer Journal
sections.content: Uploads and downloads are recorded by the main process before bytes begin moving. The journal retains destination, direction, byte totals, region, outcome, errors, timestamps, and checksum evidence where S3 returns it. It survives renderer reloads and unclean application exits; transfer observability is fail-open, so a local journal write problem never blocks the AWS operation.
tips: Open Operate → Speed → Transfer engine to inspect the latest 100 transfer records.
Clear finished removes completed, failed, and cancelled history while retaining active or resumable work.
A transfer with an unknown source size says Size unavailable instead of displaying a false zero-byte total.

sections.heading: Recovery Semantics
sections.content: Local multipart uploads retain their S3 upload ID and restart automatically after credentials become available. On the next launch, unfinished journal rows are marked Interrupted; a matching persisted multipart upload is labelled resumable. Missing local source files and explicitly cancelled uploads are never restarted. Downloads write to an isolated .s3console-part file next to the destination; its resume record (bucket, key, ETag, size) is kept in the app's data folder. Resume in Transfers continues with an S3 byte-range request only after a HeadObject check confirms that bucket, key, ETag, and size still match; stale or untrusted partials are discarded. The partial is kept whenever a retry could finish the download (a dropped connection, throttling or a server error, expired or wrong credentials, access or KMS denied, a full disk, quitting the app); if the finished file cannot replace the destination because another app has it open, the verified copy is kept and the error says where it is. Cancel in Transfers and failures a retry cannot fix (deleted object, object changed since the download started, failed verification) remove it, and an archived object is refused before any file is created.

sections.heading: Integrity and Limits
sections.content: Completed multipart uploads show checksum verification only when the upload worker and S3 provide checksum evidence. Transfer history is capped at 500 records and the UI returns the newest 100, preventing an unbounded local database. History is local to this application installation and is not an AWS billing or CloudTrail record.

sections.heading: Fast Folder and Page Navigation
sections.content: Browse predicts likely navigation without changing S3 semantics. Hovering or focusing a folder warms its first page; in paged mode loading a page also warms the next page, and in continuous mode the next page is requested about 300 rows before you reach the end. Cached pages remain scoped to profile context, region, bucket, prefix, page token, and page size. A failed or replaced Local Index continuation token is never sent to live S3.
tips: The status strip identifies whether a page came from Live S3 or the Local Index and says how much of the folder is loaded ("2 objects", "1,204 of 10,000 loaded"). Run "Show request timing" from the command palette to also see the measured time of each listing request; run it again to hide it.
Use the Local Index for Inventory-backed navigation of buckets with millions of objects.
Refresh always remains available when you need current remote state rather than the cached page.

sections.heading: Continuous Scrolling
sections.content: Continuous scrolling is the default list mode. Each ListObjectsV2 request returns up to 1,000 keys (the S3 maximum, so the fewest billable LIST requests per object), and the next page loads as you approach the bottom. Rows are windowed: only the rows in view plus a small margin are in the page, so 100,000 loaded rows scroll as smoothly as 100. The footer reads, for example, "12,400 objects loaded · more available"; Load more fetches one page on demand, and a failed page keeps what is already loaded and offers Retry.
tips: Switch between Continuous and Pages with the toggle in the list footer or the command palette; the choice is remembered.
While a filter is active, more pages load only when you ask (Load more or Load all) so a sparse match can never walk an entire huge prefix.
Refresh restarts from the first page with one LIST request; uploads and deletes re-list the pages you already loaded so your position is kept.
When the folder is served by the Local Index, pages come from SQLite and cost no S3 requests.

sections.heading: Sorting, Selection and Load All
sections.content: Column sorting, the filter and Select all apply to loaded rows. While more objects are available the footer says so and offers Load all…, which first shows an inline cost preflight — the maximum number of ListObjectsV2 requests and their price at the bundled regional LIST rate (0 requests when the Local Index serves the folder) — and then loads pages until the folder ends or 100,000 objects are loaded. Stop cancels between pages.
tips: Shift+click a checkbox to select a range; Shift+Arrow extends the selection from the keyboard.
Load all is read-only. It never changes objects; it only lists them.

sections.heading: Gallery View
sections.content: The List | Gallery toggle beside Continuous | Pages draws the loaded objects as a grid of cards: images (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .svg, .avif, .bmp) show a thumbnail, videos (.mp4, .webm, .mov) and everything else show a file-type icon, with the name, size and date under each card. The choice is remembered per bucket. Thumbnails are fetched only for cards that scroll into view, at most 6 at a time, through the same object preview used by the Preview modal: there is no server-side thumbnailing, so each thumbnail is a HeadObject and a GetObject of the whole object, which Buckets then downscales to a 256 px thumbnail. Only images in Standard-priced storage (S3 Standard, Reduced Redundancy, Express One Zone) up to 5 MB load on their own, and automatic loading stops once a folder view has fetched 50 MB: Load more thumbnails in the footer allows another 50 MB. Standard images of 5–10 MB and images in Intelligent-Tiering show Click to load; Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval images show Click to load (retrieval fee); images over 10 MB and Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive images keep their icon. The footer badge reads N GETs · X MB · est $Y: requests at each object's storage-class price, per-GB retrieval fees, and internet data transfer out for every byte downloaded. Cards are windowed like table rows, so 10,000 loaded objects scroll smoothly.
tips: Selection, Shift+click ranges, arrow / Home / End / Page keys (Shift extends the selection), the right-click menu (including Edit in local app), Preview, Download and Delete work exactly as in the table.
Scrolling back to a card you already saw costs nothing: the downscaled thumbnails stay cached for the session (up to 3,000). Opening Preview fetches the object again.
The estimate assumes internet transfer at $0.09/GB. Transfer inside the same Region, and the account's free monthly allowance, can make the bill lower.
Video posters would need the whole file, so videos keep an icon; click the card to play it in the Preview modal.

sections.heading: Responsive Interaction
sections.content: Object models and row actions are memoized so transfer progress, inspector activity, and unrelated dialogs do not rebuild every visible row. Tooltips share one provider per table instead of mounting one for every action, and filter evaluation is deferred so typing retains priority. Dragging files over Browse displays the exact target prefix before upload.

sections.heading: Release 2.7.4 Results
sections.content: Measured 8/27/2026, 11:28:22 AM UTC on Apple M2 Max (Darwin 24.1.0, arm64, 32 GiB RAM). Startup reached the mounted production application shell in 978.3 ms median and 1045.9 ms p95 across 10 isolated launches. A 50,000-object deterministic bucket displayed its first 100 rows in 196 ms; its prefetched next page displayed in 134.2 ms. Renderer heap after page two was 132.6 MiB.

sections.heading: Transfer Pipeline
sections.content: A byte-verified 128 MiB local streamed copy measured 1513.6 MiB/s median and 1708.7 MiB/s p95 across 5 runs. This is the local Node stream pipeline ceiling, not an S3 throughput promise. Real transfers depend on network capacity, AWS region, object size, concurrency, encryption, checksum work, and service throttling.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.content: Run npm run benchmark:performance from the source checkout. The harness rebuilds main and renderer, launches the production Electron application with fresh user-data directories, exercises the real renderer/preload/query/table path against a deterministic mock backend, verifies local transfer bytes, and regenerates both the in-app dataset and docs/performance/BENCHMARKS.md.
tips: Startup measurements are repeated launches with normal operating-system caches; they are not laboratory cold boots.
The large-bucket result isolates application overhead and does not include public-internet or AWS API latency.
Run release-candidate measurements on macOS, Windows, and Linux before advertising cross-platform figures.

sections.heading: Live AWS Benchmarks
sections.content: scripts/live-benchmark.mjs measures real-network behaviour against a bucket you choose: first-page ListObjectsV2 latency, prefix enumeration rate (objects per second), and key-search time from a Local Index database versus a live ListObjectsV2 scan. It is opt-in and never runs in CI: it refuses to start unless BUCKETS_LIVE_BENCH_BUCKET and an AWS profile (AWS_PROFILE or --profile) are set, uses read-only S3 calls only, caps the number of LIST requests, and writes docs/performance/LIVE_BENCHMARKS.md with the machine, operating system and region.
steps: Pick a test bucket you can list (ideally millions of objects) and an AWS profile with s3:ListBucket.
Run BUCKETS_LIVE_BENCH_BUCKET=my-bucket AWS_PROFILE=bench node scripts/live-benchmark.mjs --region us-east-1.
Optionally add --index-db <path to inventory.db> to compare Local Index search with live search.
Review docs/performance/LIVE_BENCHMARKS.md before publishing any figure.
tips: The run prints the maximum LIST request count before it starts; --max-pages lowers the cap.
Repeat on each operating system and region you intend to quote.

pages.title: Review AWS Cost & Permissions Before Running

sections.heading: What the Preflight Protects
sections.content: Before Buckets starts an explicit AWS action that can create charges, it opens a cost and permission review. The review names the AWS Region and resource, lists the IAM actions needed by that workflow, separates one-time and recurring estimates, and links to the official AWS pricing page. The AWS request is not sent until you check the acknowledgement and continue.
tips: Cancel closes the review without sending the billable AWS operation.
Read-only profile guardrails still apply after approval; cost approval never bypasses IAM or production protections.

sections.heading: How Estimates Are Calculated
sections.content: S3 upload and sync estimates use the selected Region's bundled S3 Standard storage and request rates plus the byte and object counts available from the preview. Athena uses $5 per TB scanned with its 10 MB minimum. CloudFront invalidation displays a range because Buckets cannot know how much of the account-wide monthly free path allowance has already been used. Lambda invocation displays a range because Free Tier, billed duration, architecture, and account aggregation are not available locally.
tips: A usage-dependent label is intentional: the app will not turn an unknown quantity into a false $0.00 estimate.
An unrecognized new AWS Region shows rate unavailable and links to AWS pricing instead of silently borrowing another Region's rate.

sections.heading: What Is Included
sections.content: Preflights cover uploads, folder synchronization, archived-object restore, S3 Select, Batch Operations, Inventory, Intelligent-Tiering, PII/security scans, Athena queries, Glue catalog creation, CloudFront distributions and invalidations, site publishing, CloudFront Function changes, Lambda deployment and invocation, S3 Tables maintenance, S3 Vectors semantic queries, and Bedrock Knowledge Base creation or ingestion.

sections.heading: What Can Change the Actual Bill
sections.content: The estimate uses public USD on-demand prices reviewed on the date shown in the dialog. It cannot apply your taxes, credits, private pricing, Free Tier balance, month-to-date tier usage, retries, or downstream work caused by Lambda and event rules. KMS requests, cross-Region transfer, replication, retrieval, logging, and unusually large multipart operations can add charges. AWS service pricing pages remain the billing authority.
steps: Confirm that the displayed Region and resource match your intent.
Verify the listed IAM actions against the active role and resource policies.
Review both the one-time and monthly rows; do not treat a zero setup fee as zero future usage cost.
Open the AWS pricing link when the quantity or Region rate is unavailable.
Acknowledge the estimate and continue, or cancel without running the operation.

sections.heading: Why Ordinary Browsing Does Not Interrupt You
sections.content: AWS can charge small request fees for passive reads such as listing buckets and objects. Prompting before every background refresh would prevent Browse from functioning like a file-transfer application. Buckets therefore gates explicit user-initiated cost-creating workflows and documents that ordinary browse, preview, metrics, and refresh calls can still contribute AWS request, retrieval, KMS, or transfer charges.

pages.title: AI Agent Access (MCP): A Safe S3 Gateway for Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Cursor

sections.heading: What AI Agent Access Does
sections.content: Buckets can act as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so AI agents such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Cursor can list, read, search, summarise and — with your approval — write S3 objects. The agent talks to a small launcher that Buckets installs in your user data folder; the launcher forwards each call to the running app over a private local socket. The app performs every AWS request with your saved profile, so the agent never receives access keys, secret keys, session tokens or SSO tokens.
tips: Agent access is off by default and only works while Buckets is running.
Reads are answered immediately; put, copy and delete always wait for a person to approve them in Buckets.
Every call, including denied and blocked ones, is written to the local audit log.

sections.heading: Turn On Agent Access
sections.content: Open Operate, scroll to AI agent access (MCP), tick the saved profiles agents may use, choose a mode for each, optionally restrict buckets and prefixes, then switch on Allow AI agents to connect and save. Buckets starts a local gateway that listens only on a Unix domain socket (macOS and Linux) or a named pipe (Windows) — never on a network port.
steps: Open the command palette and run “AI agent access (MCP)”.
Tick each saved profile to expose and pick Read-only or Read-write with approval.
Optionally enter allowlist lines such as my-bucket or reports/agent-output/ prefixed by the bucket name.
Switch on Allow AI agents to connect and choose Turn on and save.
Copy the configuration for your agent from Connect an agent.

sections.heading: Connect Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor
sections.content: The Connect an agent tabs show copy-ready configuration with the exact paths for this computer. By default the agent starts the installed Buckets executable in Node mode (environment variable ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1) with the launcher script from your Buckets data folder, so nothing else needs to be installed. Choose Use system Node.js to run the launcher with Node.js 18 or later instead; Microsoft Store installs always use Node.js because their executable cannot be started by path. Claude Code uses a claude mcp add command; Claude Desktop and Cursor use an mcpServers JSON entry.
tips: macOS example: claude mcp add --env ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 --transport stdio --scope user buckets -- /Applications/Buckets.app/Contents/MacOS/Buckets '…/S3Console/mcp/launcher/bucketsMcpLauncher.js'
The launcher copy is refreshed every time the gateway starts, so app updates never require reconfiguring the agent.
AppImage users get the AppImage file path, which stays stable while the mount point changes on each launch.

sections.heading: Profiles, Modes and Allowlists
sections.content: Only the saved profiles you tick are visible to agents. Read-only profiles refuse put, copy and delete before anything is shown to you. Read-write profiles allow those tools but still require approval for every call. An allowlist entry is either a bucket name (the whole bucket) or bucket/prefix; when a bucket only has prefix entries, listing, search, reads and writes must stay under those prefixes and whole-bucket summaries are refused. Buckets' Guardrails also apply: a profile in read-only mode, including every profile whose name contains the word prod or production, blocks agent writes until you temporarily unlock it in Operate → Guardrails. After you approve, Buckets checks these settings again before writing, so switching a profile to read-only, narrowing its allowlist or turning agent access off while a prompt is open stops the write. On AWS, an approved write only goes through if the object is still in the state you reviewed (new, or the same version you saw); otherwise nothing is written.
tips: When more than one profile is exposed, agents pass the profile name with each call; list_buckets tells them which profiles exist and their modes.
Deleting a saved profile removes it from agent access automatically.

sections.heading: Approving Agent Writes
sections.content: When an agent calls put_object_text, copy_object or delete_objects, Buckets brings its window forward and shows the exact action: agent name, profile, bucket, Region, keys, byte counts, whether an existing object will be overwritten, the bucket's versioning status, a preview of text being written, and the same cost estimate used by Buckets' cost preflight. Approve runs the request once. Deny, closing the dialog, or letting the timer run out (120 seconds by default, configurable from 15 to 600) rejects it, and the agent receives a clear explanation telling it not to retry without asking you.
tips: Deleting from a versioned bucket adds delete markers; earlier versions remain recoverable. Deleting a specific version id is permanent, and the dialog says so.
At most three agent actions can wait for approval at once; further writes are rejected until you decide.
If an agent cancels a call while the prompt is open, the prompt closes and nothing is changed.

sections.heading: Available Tools
sections.content: list_buckets, list_objects (prefix, delimiter and up to 1,000 entries per page), head_object, read_object_text (UTF-8 text types only, up to 1 MiB, with a truncated flag), search_objects (uses the local S3 Inventory index when the bucket has one and the exposed profile passes a one-key list-permission check, otherwise scans up to 10,000 keys), presign_get (1 hour by default, 7 days maximum), bucket_summary (Region, versioning, object count, size by storage class and an estimated monthly storage cost from the inventory index, CloudWatch storage metrics or a capped sample), put_object_text (up to 1 MiB, approval), copy_object (up to 5 GiB, approval) and delete_objects (up to 100 objects, approval).
tips: Each tool publishes MCP annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint) and a JSON Schema for its arguments.
Agent calls are rate limited: about 120 reads and 6 writes per minute with short bursts.

sections.heading: Audit Log and Activity
sections.content: Recent agent activity in the panel lists the latest calls with agent, tool, profile, target and decision (allowed, approved, denied, timeout, blocked, rate-limited or error). The same calls are appended to the Local audit log in Operate → Guardrails as operations named MCP <tool>, which you can search and export. Records contain bucket and key names, byte counts and decisions only — never object contents, written text, presigned URLs or credentials.

sections.heading: Security Model
sections.content: The launcher and the app share a random 256-bit token stored in your user data folder with owner-only permissions, and they prove to each other that they know it with a challenge–response exchange over fresh random values: the token itself never travels over the socket, the app has to prove itself before the launcher sends anything else, and a recorded exchange cannot be replayed. The app checks proofs in constant time and drops connections that do not authenticate within five seconds. The socket file and its folder are owner-only on macOS and Linux, and Windows named pipes reject writes from other users. Rotate token issues a new token and disconnects every connected agent; configured agents keep working because the launcher reads the new token on its next connection. Turning access off stops the gateway, removes its endpoint file and denies any pending approvals.
tips: Any program running as your user can read the token, just as it could read your AWS configuration files; the gateway protects against other users and keeps credentials inside Buckets.
Presigned URLs embed the access key id (and the session token for temporary credentials) but never the secret key; anyone holding the URL can download that one object until it expires.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.content: If an agent reports that Buckets is not running or agent access is off, open Buckets and confirm the panel shows On. If the status shows Not running, the error explains why the gateway could not start (for example, an unwritable data folder). Use the refresh button to update the connected-agent count. A token error after rotating means an old launcher process is still connected; restart the MCP client. If the agent says the local Buckets endpoint could not prove it knows the agent token and retrying does not help, quit and restart Buckets: another program may be occupying its local endpoint, and the launcher refuses to talk to it. On Windows Store installs, install Node.js 18 or later and use the system Node.js configuration.
